result.statement: Two unequal magnitudes being set out, if from the greater there be subtracted a magnitude greater than its half, and from that which is left a magnitude greater than its half, and if this process be repeated continually, there will be left some magnitude which will be less than the lesser magnitude set out.
result.proof:
**Step 1.** Let AB and C be the two unequal magnitudes set out, and let AB be the greater. Throughout, for any magnitude X of the kind considered, ½X denotes its half, so that X = ½X + ½X; and to say that one magnitude exceeds another means that the greater is the lesser together with some further magnitude (the excess). It is to be shown that, if from AB there is subtracted a magnitude greater than ½AB, from the remainder a magnitude greater than its half, and so on continually, a magnitude less than C will at some stage be left.

**Step 2.** (Halves of unequals.) If X > Y, then ½X > ½Y. For ½X is either equal to, less than, or greater than ½Y. If ½X = ½Y, then, equals being added to equals, ½X + ½X = ½Y + ½Y, i.e. X = Y [CN2], which is impossible. If ½X < ½Y, let ½Y = ½X + T; then Y = ½Y + ½Y = (½X + ½X) + (T + T) = X + (T + T), so X is a part of Y and Y > X [CN5], which is impossible. Therefore ½X > ½Y.

**Step 3.** (Remainder after subtracting more than half.) If from a magnitude Y there is subtracted a part Y₂ greater than ½Y, the remainder Y₁ is less than ½Y. For let Y₂ = ½Y + T; then Y₁ + ½Y + T = Y₁ + Y₂ = Y = ½Y + ½Y, and subtracting ½Y from both [CN3], Y₁ + T = ½Y; so Y₁ is a part of ½Y, whence Y₁ < ½Y [CN5].

**Step 4.** (Remainder after subtracting not more than half.) If from a magnitude X there is subtracted a part X₂ not greater than ½X, the remainder X₁ is not less than ½X. For if X₂ = ½X, then from X₁ + X₂ = ½X + ½X, subtracting equals [CN3], X₁ = ½X. If X₂ < ½X, let ½X = X₂ + T; then X₁ + X₂ = ½X + ½X = X₂ + (½X + T), and subtracting X₂ from both [CN3], X₁ = ½X + T, so that X₁ > ½X [CN5].

**Step 5.** (Lemma.) If X > Y, and from X there is subtracted a magnitude not greater than ½X while from Y there is subtracted a magnitude greater than ½Y, then the remainder X₁ of X is greater than the remainder Y₁ of Y. For X₁ is not less than ½X (Step 4), ½X > ½Y (Step 2), and ½Y > Y₁ (Step 3); hence X₁ > Y₁.

**Step 6.** Since AB and C are magnitudes of the same kind, they have a ratio to one another, and therefore C, being multiplied, is capable of exceeding AB [D5.4]. Let C be multiplied until its multiple exceeds AB, and let DE be this multiple, so that DE > AB and DE is made up of parts DF, FG, GE, …, each equal to C; let n be the number of these parts. If n were 1, DE would be equal to C, which is less than AB, contrary to DE > AB; therefore n ≥ 2.

**Step 7.** From AB subtract BH greater than ½AB, leaving AH; from AH subtract HK greater than ½AH, leaving AK; and let this process be continued until n − 1 subtractions have been made, so that the pieces subtracted from AB together with the final remainder are equal in multitude to the n parts of DE. Write A₀ = AB, A₁ = AH, A₂ = AK, …, Aₙ₋₁ for the successive remainders; thus for each k from 1 to n − 1, Aₖ is what is left of Aₖ₋₁ after subtracting from it a magnitude greater than ½Aₖ₋₁.

**Step 8.** Correspondingly, from DE take away its last part GE (equal to C), leaving W₁, made up of n − 1 parts equal to C; from W₁ take away its last part FG, leaving W₂, made up of n − 2 parts; and so on. Write W₀ = DE, and in general let Wₖ be the magnitude made up of the first n − k parts of DE, so that Wₙ₋₁ = DF = C. For each k from 1 to n − 1 we have Wₖ₋₁ = Wₖ + C, and Wₖ, consisting of n − k ≥ 1 parts, is equal to C when n − k = 1 and is greater than C when n − k ≥ 2, C being then a part of it [CN5].

**Step 9.** The part C taken away from Wₖ₋₁ is not greater than ½Wₖ₋₁ (1 ≤ k ≤ n − 1). For if Wₖ = C, then Wₖ₋₁ = C + C, so that C is ½Wₖ₋₁. If Wₖ > C, let Wₖ = C + T; then Wₖ₋₁ = Wₖ + C = (C + C) + T, so C + C is a part of Wₖ₋₁ and Wₖ₋₁ > C + C [CN5]; hence by Step 2, ½Wₖ₋₁ > ½(C + C) = C.

**Step 10.** I say that Wₖ > Aₖ for every k from 0 to n − 1. For k = 0 this is W₀ = DE > AB = A₀ (Step 6). Suppose Wₖ₋₁ > Aₖ₋₁ for some k with 1 ≤ k ≤ n − 1. From Wₖ₋₁ there is subtracted C, which is not greater than ½Wₖ₋₁ (Step 9), leaving Wₖ; from Aₖ₋₁ there is subtracted a magnitude greater than ½Aₖ₋₁ (Step 7), leaving Aₖ. Therefore, by the Lemma of Step 5, Wₖ > Aₖ. Proceeding thus from k = 1 to k = n − 1, we obtain Wₖ > Aₖ for every k up to n − 1.

**Step 11.** Taking k = n − 1, Wₙ₋₁ > Aₙ₋₁. But Wₙ₋₁ is the single part DF, which is equal to C. Therefore C > Aₙ₋₁; that is, the magnitude Aₙ₋₁ left after the (n − 1)-th subtraction is less than C, the lesser magnitude set out.

**Step 12.** Therefore, two unequal magnitudes being set out, if from the greater there be subtracted a magnitude greater than its half, and from that which is left a magnitude greater than its half, and if this process be repeated continually, there will be left some magnitude which will be less than the lesser magnitude set out. Q.E.D.

result.statement: If, when the less of two unequal magnitudes is continually subtracted in turn from the greater, that which is left never measures the one before it, the magnitudes will be incommensurable.
result.proof:
**Step 1.** Let AB, CD be two unequal magnitudes, of which AB is the less, and suppose that, when the less is continually subtracted in turn from the greater, that which is left never measures the one before it. That is: let AB, measuring FD, leave CF less than itself; by hypothesis CF does not measure AB. Let CF, measuring BG, leave AG less than itself; by hypothesis AG does not measure CF. Let AG, measuring CK, leave KF less than itself; by hypothesis KF does not measure AG; and let this process be repeated continually. Because no remainder measures the one before it, each subtraction leaves a remainder, so the process never comes to an end. I say that AB, CD are incommensurable.

**Step 2.** Suppose, if possible, that AB, CD are commensurable. Then by D10.1.1 they are measured by the same measure; let E be a magnitude which measures both AB and CD.

**Step 3.** E measures every magnitude subtracted and every remainder in the process. For E measures AB, and AB measures FD, so that FD is a multiple of AB (D5.2) and AB is a multiple of E; hence FD is made up of magnitudes each equal to E, that is, E measures FD. And since E measures the whole CD and also the part FD taken from it, CD being made up of a certain number of magnitudes equal to E and FD of a smaller number of them, the remainder CF is made up of the rest; therefore E measures CF. Again, E measures CF and CF measures BG, hence E measures BG; and E measures the whole AB and the part BG, hence E measures the remainder AG. In the same manner E measures CK and therefore the remainder KF; and so on: at every stage E measures both magnitudes concerned, therefore it measures the multiple subtracted, and therefore it measures what is left. Thus E measures each remainder CF, AG, KF, ... that arises in the process.

**Step 4.** Each subtraction made on the side of CD takes away more than half. For FD is measured by AB, so that FD is either equal to AB or a multiple of AB (D5.2), and hence FD is not less than AB (CN5); but CF is less than AB; therefore FD is greater than CF. Since CD is made up of CF and FD, and FD is greater than CF, FD is greater than half of CD. Likewise CK, being measured by AG, is not less than AG, while KF is less than AG; so CK is greater than KF, and therefore CK is greater than half of CF. And so on continually: at every stage the multiple subtracted from CD, CF, KF, ... exceeds the remainder left, and hence is greater than half of the magnitude from which it is taken.

**Step 5.** E is less than CD. For E measures AB, so that E is either equal to AB or a part of AB (D5.1), whence E is not greater than AB (CN5); and AB is less than CD. Thus CD, E are two unequal magnitudes of which CD is the greater. Now from CD there has been subtracted FD, greater than its half, leaving CF; from CF there has been subtracted CK, greater than its half, leaving KF; and this process is repeated continually without end (Steps 1 and 4). Therefore, by 10.1, there will be left some magnitude less than E. Let L be this remainder; it is one of the remainders CF, KF, ... of the process.

**Step 6.** By Step 3, E measures L. Hence L is either equal to E or a multiple of E (D5.2), so that L is not less than E (CN5). But by Step 5, L is less than E. Thus the greater magnitude E would measure the less magnitude L, which is impossible.

**Step 7.** Therefore no magnitude can measure both AB and CD; that is, AB, CD cannot have any common measure. Hence, by D10.1.1, AB and CD are incommensurable. Q.E.D.

result.statement: Given two commensurable magnitudes, to find their greatest common measure.
result.proof:
**Step 1.** Let AB, CD be the two given commensurable magnitudes, and let AB be the less of them (if they are equal, each measures the other, and the argument of Steps 2–3 applies without change). Since AB, CD are commensurable, there is some magnitude which measures both of them (D10.1.1); it is required to find the greatest such magnitude. Now either AB measures CD, or it does not.

**Step 2.** First let AB measure CD. Since AB also measures itself, AB is a common measure of AB and CD.

**Step 3.** AB is moreover the greatest common measure. For no magnitude greater than AB can measure AB: a magnitude which measures another is contained in it a whole number of times, and so is either equal to it or a part of it (D5.1), and a part is less than the whole (CN5); thus any magnitude measuring AB is not greater than AB. Hence no magnitude greater than AB measures both AB and CD, and AB is the greatest common measure required.

**Step 4.** Next let AB not measure CD. Let the less be continually subtracted in turn from the greater: AB from CD as many times as possible, then the remainder from AB as many times as possible, and so on. It cannot happen that every remainder fails to measure the one before it; for then, by 10.2, AB and CD would be incommensurable, whereas they are commensurable (D10.1.1). Therefore at some stage a remainder measures the one before it. For definiteness let this happen at the third stage (the reasoning is identical however many stages are required): let AB, measuring ED, leave EC less than itself; let EC, measuring FB, leave AF less than itself; and let AF measure CE. Then CD is made up of CE and ED, and AB is made up of AF and FB.

**Step 5.** Since AF measures CE, and CE measures FB, AF also measures FB; for FB is made up of magnitudes each equal to CE, and each of these is made up of magnitudes each equal to AF.

**Step 6.** AF measures FB (Step 5) and also measures itself, AF; hence AF measures the whole AB, since the magnitudes equal to AF which make up FB, together with AF itself, make up AB.

**Step 7.** AF measures AB (Step 6), and AB measures ED; hence, as in Step 5, AF measures ED. But AF also measures CE (Step 4); hence AF measures the whole CD, which is made up of CE and ED.

**Step 8.** Therefore AF measures both AB and CD, and is a common measure of them.

**Step 9.** I say that AF is also the greatest common measure. For, if not, let G be a magnitude greater than AF which measures both AB and CD. Since G measures AB, and AB measures ED, G measures ED (as in Step 5). But G also measures the whole CD; therefore G measures the remainder CE as well, since when the magnitudes equal to G which make up ED are taken away from those which make up CD, those which are left make up CE. Again, since G measures CE, and CE measures FB, G measures FB; and G measures the whole AB; therefore, in the same way, G measures the remainder AF. Thus G, which is greater than AF, measures AF; but this is impossible, for a magnitude measuring AF is either equal to AF or a part of AF (D5.1), and hence not greater than AF (CN5).

**Step 10.** Therefore no magnitude greater than AF measures both AB and CD; and AF, which measures both, is their greatest common measure. Thus, given two commensurable magnitudes AB, CD, their greatest common measure has been found. Q.E.F.

**Step 11.** (Corollary.) The hypothesis G > AF was used in Step 9 only in its final sentence; the preceding reasoning shows that any magnitude which measures both AB and CD measures AF. Hence, if a magnitude measures two magnitudes, it also measures their greatest common measure.

result.statement: Given three commensurable magnitudes, to find their greatest common measure.
result.proof:
**Statement:** Given three commensurable magnitudes, to find their greatest common measure.

Let A, B, C be the three given commensurable magnitudes; thus it is required to find their greatest common measure.

**Step 1.** Since A, B, C are commensurable, they are measured by one and the same measure (D10.1.1); in particular A and B are commensurable. By 10.3 let D be the greatest common measure of A and B, so that D measures A and D measures B. Then D either measures C or does not measure it.

**Step 2.** First, let D measure C. Then D measures each of A, B, C, so D is a common measure of A, B, C. I say that it is also the greatest. For, if not, there is some magnitude F greater than D which measures A, B, C. Since F measures A and B, it also measures their greatest common measure D (10.3, Porism). But a magnitude which measures another is a part of it, the less of the greater (D5.1), so F would be less than D, whereas it was supposed greater; which is impossible. Therefore D is the greatest common measure of A, B, C.

**Step 3.** Next, let D not measure C. I say first that C and D are commensurable. Since A, B, C are commensurable, let some magnitude G measure A, B, C (D10.1.1). Since G measures A and B, it also measures D, the greatest common measure of A and B (10.3, Porism). And G measures C. Therefore C and D are measured by the same measure G, so C and D are commensurable (D10.1.1).

**Step 4.** By 10.3 let E be the greatest common measure of C and D. Then E measures D, and D measures each of A and B; hence A and B are multiples of D, and D is a multiple of E (D5.2), so that A and B are each made up of magnitudes equal to E; therefore E measures A and E measures B. And E measures C. Therefore E is a common measure of A, B, C.

**Step 5.** I say that E is also the greatest. For, if not, let F be a magnitude greater than E which measures A, B, C. Since F measures A and B, it measures their greatest common measure D (10.3, Porism). Since F measures D and also measures C, it measures the greatest common measure of C and D, namely E (10.3, Porism). But then F, measuring E, is a part of E, the less of the greater (D5.1), so F is less than E, whereas it was supposed greater; which is impossible. Therefore E is the greatest common measure of A, B, C.

**Step 6.** Therefore, in either case, the greatest common measure of the three given commensurable magnitudes A, B, C has been found. Q.E.F.

**Porism.** From this it is manifest that, if a magnitude measure three magnitudes, it also measures their greatest common measure: for such a magnitude measures A and B, hence D (10.3, Porism), and measures D and C, hence E (10.3, Porism), as shown in Steps 2 and 5.

result.statement: Commensurable magnitudes have to one another the ratio which a number has to a number.
result.proof:
**Step 1.** Let A and B be commensurable magnitudes. By D10.1.1, commensurable magnitudes are those which are measured by the same measure; therefore some magnitude measures both A and B. Let C be such a magnitude, so that C measures A and C measures B.

**Step 2.** As many times as C measures A, so many units let there be in the number D; and as many times as C measures B, so many units let there be in the number E [D7.2, a number being a multitude composed of units]. Thus D and E are numbers; A is made up of as many magnitudes equal to C as there are units in D, and B is made up of as many magnitudes equal to C as there are units in E.

**Step 3.** Since C measures A, C is a part of A [D5.1]; and since the unit measures the number D, the unit is a part of D [D7.3]. Now C measures A according to the units in D, while the unit measures D according to the units in it; hence the unit measures D the same number of times that C measures A. Therefore C is the same part of A that the unit is of D, and consequently, as C is to A, so is the unit to D [D7.20].

**Step 4.** Since, as C is to A, so is the unit to D, therefore, inversely, as A is to C, so is D to the unit [5.7, Porism].

**Step 5.** Again, since C measures B according to the units in E, while the unit measures E according to the units in it, the unit measures E the same number of times that C measures B. Therefore C is the same part of B [D5.1] that the unit is of E [D7.3]; hence, as C is to B, so is the unit to E [D7.20].

**Step 6.** There are now three magnitudes A, C, B and three others D, unit, E equal to them in multitude, which taken two and two are in the same ratio: as A is to C, so is D to the unit (Step 4), and as C is to B, so is the unit to E (Step 5). Therefore, ex aequali, as A is to B, so is D to E [5.22].

**Step 7.** Therefore the commensurable magnitudes A and B have to one another the ratio which the number D has to the number E. Q.E.D.

result.statement: If two magnitudes have to one another the ratio which a number has to a number, the magnitudes will be commensurable.
result.proof:
## Proposition 10.6
**Statement:** If two magnitudes have to one another the ratio which a number has to a number, the magnitudes will be commensurable.

Let A, B be two magnitudes, and let A have to B the ratio which the number D has to the number E. I say that A and B are commensurable.

**Step 1.** Since D is a number, it is a multitude composed of units [D7.2]. Let A be divided into as many equal parts as there are units in D, and let C be equal to one of these parts. Then A is made up of as many magnitudes equal to C as there are units in D; hence C measures A, so that C is a part of A and A is a multiple of C [D5.1, D5.2].

**Step 2.** Let F be made up of as many magnitudes equal to C as there are units in E (that is, C added to itself as many times as there are units in E). Then C measures F, so that C is a part of F and F is a multiple of C [D5.1, D5.2].

**Step 3.** The unit measures D, so the unit is a part of D [D7.3]; and D contains exactly as many units as A contains magnitudes equal to C. Therefore C is the same part of A that the unit is of D; equivalently, A is the same multiple of C that D is of the unit. Hence, as A is to C, so is D to the unit [D7.20].

**Step 4.** Likewise the unit is a part of E [D7.3], and F contains exactly as many magnitudes equal to C as E contains units; therefore C is the same part of F that the unit is of E. Hence, as C is to F, so is the unit to E [D7.20].

**Step 5.** We now have three magnitudes A, C, F and three others D, the unit, E, equal to them in multitude, which taken two and two are in the same ratio: A : C = D : unit (Step 3) and C : F = unit : E (Step 4). Therefore, ex aequali, as A is to F, so is D to E [5.22].

**Step 6.** But by hypothesis, as D is to E, so is A to B. Therefore, since ratios which are the same with the same ratio are also the same with one another, as A is to B, so is A to F [5.11].

**Step 7.** Thus A has the same ratio to each of the magnitudes B and F; therefore B is equal to F [5.9].

**Step 8.** Now C measures F (Step 2), and F is equal to B; therefore C measures B. But C also measures A (Step 1). Therefore C is a common measure of A and B, so A and B are measured by the same measure, and hence A and B are commensurable [D10.1.1].

Therefore, if two magnitudes have to one another the ratio which a number has to a number, the magnitudes are commensurable. Q.E.D.

*Path note:* the "same multiple" clause of D7.20 is applied directly in Step 3 to obtain A : C = D : unit, so no inversion step (5.7 Porism) is needed; this is the most direct route to the ex aequali configuration of Step 5.

**USED:** D7.2, D5.1, D5.2, D7.3, D7.20, 5.22, 5.11, 5.9, D10.1.1

result.statement: Incommensurable magnitudes have not to one another the ratio which a number has to a number.
result.proof:
**Step 1.** Let A and B be two incommensurable magnitudes; that is, by definition, A and B cannot have any common measure [D10.1.1].

**Step 2.** I say that A has not to B the ratio which a number has to a number.

**Step 3.** For suppose, if possible, that A has to B the ratio which some number has to some number.

**Step 4.** Then, since the two magnitudes A and B have to one another the ratio which a number has to a number, the magnitudes A and B are commensurable [10.6]; that is, A and B are measured by some common measure [D10.1.1].

**Step 5.** But by hypothesis A and B are incommensurable, so that they cannot have any common measure [D10.1.1]. Thus A and B are both measured by a common measure and cannot have any common measure, which is impossible.

**Step 6.** Therefore the supposition in Step 3 is false; hence A has not to B the ratio which a number has to a number.

Therefore incommensurable magnitudes have not to one another the ratio which a number has to a number. Q.E.D.

result.statement: If two magnitudes have not to one another the ratio which a number has to a number, the magnitudes will be incommensurable.
result.proof:
## Proposition 10.8
**Statement:** If two magnitudes have not to one another the ratio which a number has to a number, the magnitudes will be incommensurable.

**Step 1.** Let A and B be two magnitudes which have not to one another the ratio which a number has to a number. I say that A and B are incommensurable.

**Step 2.** Suppose, if possible, that A and B are commensurable, that is, that there exists some magnitude which measures both A and B [D10.1.1].

**Step 3.** Then, since A and B are commensurable magnitudes, they have to one another the ratio which a number has to a number [10.5].

**Step 4.** But by hypothesis A has not to B the ratio which a number has to a number. This is impossible; therefore A and B cannot be commensurable.

**Step 5.** Hence A and B cannot have any common measure, that is, they are incommensurable [D10.1.1].

Therefore, if two magnitudes have not to one another the ratio which a number has to a number, the magnitudes will be incommensurable. Q.E.D.

**USED:** D10.1.1, 10.5

result.statement: The squares on straight lines commensurable in length have to one another the ratio which a square number has to a square number; and squares which have to one another the ratio which a square number has to a square number will also have their sides commensurable in length. But the squares on straight lines incommensurable in length have not to one another the ratio which a square number has to a square number; and squares which have not to one another the ratio which a square number has to a square number will not have their sides commensurable in length either.
result.proof:
**Statement:** The squares on straight lines commensurable in length have to one another the ratio which a square number has to a square number; and squares which have to one another the ratio which a square number has to a square number will also have their sides commensurable in length. But the squares on straight lines incommensurable in length have not to one another the ratio which a square number has to a square number; and squares which have not to one another the ratio which a square number has to a square number will not have their sides commensurable in length either.

Throughout, let A and B be two straight lines; write sq(A), sq(B) for the squares described on them, and rect(A,B) for the rectangle contained by A and B (D2.1). Steps 1–3 establish an auxiliary result used in both directions of the theorem: if A : B = C : D, where C and D are numbers, then sq(A) : sq(B) = (C·C) : (D·D).

**Step 1.** Suppose A : B = C : D, where C, D are numbers. Let E = C·C and F = D·D; these are square numbers, each being equal multiplied by equal (D7.18). Let also M = C·D. Since the number C, multiplying the two numbers C and D, makes E and M, we have E : M = C : D (7.17). Since the two numbers C and D, multiplying the number D, make M and F, we have M : F = C : D (7.18). Thus E, M, F are in continued proportion, each term having to the next the ratio C : D.

**Step 2.** The square on A and the rectangle contained by A, B are parallelograms under the same height A, standing on the bases A and B respectively; therefore sq(A) : rect(A,B) = A : B (6.1). Likewise the rectangle contained by A, B and the square on B are parallelograms under the same height B, standing on the bases A and B respectively; therefore rect(A,B) : sq(B) = A : B (6.1). Thus sq(A), rect(A,B), sq(B) are in continued proportion, each term having to the next the ratio A : B.

**Step 3.** Since A : B = C : D, Steps 1 and 2 give sq(A) : rect(A,B) = E : M and rect(A,B) : sq(B) = M : F, ratios which are the same with the same ratio being the same with one another (5.11). The three magnitudes sq(A), rect(A,B), sq(B) and the three numbers E, M, F, taken two and two, are therefore in the same ratio; hence, ex aequali, sq(A) : sq(B) = E : F (5.22). This is the auxiliary result: if A : B = C : D, then sq(A) : sq(B) = (C·C) : (D·D).

**Step 4.** (First part.) Let A and B be commensurable in length, that is, let the straight lines A and B themselves be measured by a common measure (D10.1.1). Commensurable magnitudes have to one another the ratio which a number has to a number; so A : B = C : D for some numbers C, D (10.5). By Steps 1–3, sq(A) : sq(B) = E : F, where E = C·C and F = D·D are square numbers. Therefore the squares on A and B have to one another the ratio which a square number has to a square number.

**Step 5.** (Second part.) Conversely, let sq(A) : sq(B) = E : F, where E and F are square numbers, say E = C·C and F = D·D for numbers C, D (D7.18). Given the straight line A and the numbers C, D, a straight line H can be made such that A : H = C : D (10.6, Porism).

**Step 6.** Applying Steps 1–3 to the straight lines A and H, for which A : H = C : D, we obtain sq(A) : sq(H) = E : F. But by hypothesis sq(A) : sq(B) = E : F. Therefore sq(A) : sq(H) = sq(A) : sq(B) (5.11).

**Step 7.** Any two squares are similar rectilineal figures: all their angles are right angles (D1.22) and hence equal to one another (P4), and, each square being equilateral (D1.22), the sides about the equal angles are proportional (D6.1). So the squares on the four straight lines A, H, A, B are similar and similarly described figures, and by Step 6 they are proportional. Hence the straight lines themselves are proportional: A : H = A : B (6.22).

**Step 8.** Since A : H = C : D (Step 5) and A : H = A : B (Step 7), we have A : B = C : D (5.11). Thus A has to B the ratio which a number has to a number; therefore A and B are commensurable (10.6), and since the lines themselves are commensurable, A and B are commensurable in length (D10.1.1).

**Step 9.** (Third part.) Now let A and B be incommensurable in length. If the squares on A and B had to one another the ratio which a square number has to a square number, then by Steps 5–8 the straight lines A and B would be commensurable in length, which is contrary to the hypothesis. Therefore the squares on A and B have not to one another the ratio which a square number has to a square number.

**Step 10.** (Fourth part.) Finally, let the squares on A and B not have to one another the ratio which a square number has to a square number. If A and B were commensurable in length, then by Step 4 the squares on them would have to one another the ratio which a square number has to a square number, which is contrary to the hypothesis. Therefore A and B are not commensurable in length.

Hence the squares on straight lines commensurable in length have to one another the ratio of a square number to a square number, and conversely; and the squares on straight lines incommensurable in length have not such a ratio, and conversely. Q.E.D.

result.statement: To find two straight lines incommensurable, the one in length only, and the other in square also, with an assigned straight line.
result.proof:
**Step 1.** Let A be the assigned straight line. Set out a square number B [D7.18] and a prime number C [D7.11] (for instance B = 4 and C = 3). Then B has not to C the ratio which a square number has to a square number. For if it had, then, since B is square, C would also be square [8.24], that is, C would be contained by two equal numbers p, p [D7.18]. But p·p is p added to itself as many times as there are units in p [D7.15]; since p is a number, this is more than once, so that p·p is measured by p and is greater than p [CN5]. Thus C would be measured by a number p which is neither the unit nor C itself, so that C would not be prime [D7.11], contrary to hypothesis. Therefore B has not to C the ratio which a square number has to a square number.

**Step 2.** By the Porism to 10.6, take a straight line F such that, as the number B is to the number C, so is A to F [10.6].

**Step 3.** Take D a mean proportional between A and F [6.13], so that A : D = D : F. Then A has to F the ratio duplicate of that which A has to D [D5.9]; and the square on A has to the square on D the ratio duplicate of that which A has to D, since similar rectilineal figures are to one another in the duplicate ratio of their corresponding sides [6.20]. Therefore, as A is to F, so is the square on A to the square on D. But, as A is to F, so is B to C; therefore, as B is to C, so is the square on A to the square on D [5.11].

**Step 4.** Since the square on A has to the square on D the ratio which the number B has to the number C, the square on A is commensurable with the square on D [10.6]; that is, A is commensurable in square with D [D10.1.2].

**Step 5.** Again, the square on A has not to the square on D the ratio which a square number has to a square number: for if it had, then B : C, being the same ratio [5.11], would be the ratio of a square number to a square number, which is contrary to Step 1. Therefore A is incommensurable in length with D [10.9]. Thus D is incommensurable in length only with A, being commensurable with it in square.

**Step 6.** Take E a mean proportional between A and D [6.13], so that A : E = E : D. Then A has to D the ratio duplicate of that which A has to E [D5.9], and the square on A has to the square on E the ratio duplicate of that which A has to E [6.20]; therefore, as A is to D, so is the square on A to the square on E.

**Step 7.** Now A is incommensurable in length with D (Step 5); therefore A has not to D the ratio which a number has to a number [10.7]. Hence neither has the square on A to the square on E the ratio which a number has to a number: for if the square on A had to the square on E the ratio of a number to a number, then A : D, being the same ratio, would also be the ratio of a number to a number [5.11], which is impossible. Therefore the square on A is incommensurable with the square on E [10.8]; that is, A is incommensurable in square with E [D10.1.2].

**Step 8.** Moreover A is incommensurable in length with E also. For if A were commensurable in length with E, the square on A would have to the square on E the ratio which a square number has to a square number [10.9], and hence the ratio of a number to a number, so that the square on A would be commensurable with the square on E [10.6], contrary to Step 7. Therefore E is incommensurable with A both in length and in square.

**Step 9.** Therefore two straight lines D, E have been found incommensurable with the assigned straight line A, the one (D) in length only, and the other (E) in square also. Q.E.F.

**USED:** D7.18, D7.11, D7.15, CN5, 8.24, 10.6, 6.13, D5.9, 6.20, 5.11, D10.1.2, 10.9, 10.7, 10.8

result.statement: If four magnitudes be proportional, and the first be commensurable with the second, the third will also be commensurable with the fourth; and, if the first be incommensurable with the second, the third will also be incommensurable with the fourth.
result.proof:
**Step 1.** Let A, B, C, D be four magnitudes in proportion, so that as A is to B, so is C to D.

**Step 2.** First, let A be commensurable with B. Then A has to B the ratio which a number has to a number [10.5]; let it be the ratio which the number E has to the number F.

**Step 3.** Since as A is to B, so is C to D, and as A is to B, so is E to F, therefore as C is to D, so is E to F, for ratios which are the same with the same ratio are also the same with one another [5.11].

**Step 4.** Therefore C has to D the ratio which the number E has to the number F; hence C is commensurable with D [10.6].

**Step 5.** Next, let A be incommensurable with B. Then A has not to B the ratio which a number has to a number [10.7].

**Step 6.** Suppose, if possible, that C has to D the ratio which some number G has to some number H. Since as A is to B, so is C to D, and as C is to D, so is G to H, therefore as A is to B, so is G to H [5.11]; so A would have to B the ratio which a number has to a number, which is impossible by Step 5.

**Step 7.** Therefore C has not to D the ratio which a number has to a number; hence C is incommensurable with D [10.8].

**Step 8.** Therefore, if four magnitudes be proportional, and the first be commensurable with the second, the third is also commensurable with the fourth; and, if the first be incommensurable with the second, the third is also incommensurable with the fourth. Q.E.D.

result.statement: Magnitudes commensurable with the same magnitude are commensurable with one another also.
result.proof:
**Step 1.** Let A and B be two magnitudes, each of which is commensurable with the same magnitude C. I say that A is also commensurable with B.

**Step 2.** Since A is commensurable with C, A has to C the ratio which a number has to a number [10.5]. Let that ratio be taken in its least numbers D, E [7.33], so that A : C = D : E.

**Step 3.** Since C is commensurable with B, C has to B the ratio which a number has to a number [10.5]. Let that ratio likewise be taken in its least numbers F, G [7.33], so that C : B = F : G.

**Step 4.** Given the two ratios D : E and F : G in least numbers, take numbers H, K, L in continued proportion in these given ratios, so that H : K = D : E and K : L = F : G [8.4].

**Step 5.** Since A : C = D : E and H : K = D : E, therefore A : C = H : K [5.11]. Likewise, since C : B = F : G and K : L = F : G, therefore C : B = K : L [5.11].

**Step 6.** Thus the three magnitudes A, C, B and the three numbers H, K, L, taken two and two together, are in the same ratio; therefore, ex aequali, A : B = H : L [5.22].

**Step 7.** Therefore A has to B the ratio which the number H has to the number L; hence A is commensurable with B [10.6].

**Step 8.** Therefore magnitudes commensurable with the same magnitude are commensurable with one another also. Q.E.D.

Path note: the numbers H, K, L are obtained by 8.4, which presupposes the given ratios in least numbers; hence 7.33 is invoked first. An alternative route forms H, K, L as products via 7.17 and 7.16, but 8.4 is the tool built precisely for this purpose and gives the more direct proof.

result.statement: If two magnitudes be commensurable, and the one of them be incommensurable with any magnitude, the remaining one will also be incommensurable with the same.
result.proof:
**Step 1.** Let A and B be two commensurable magnitudes, and let one of them, A, be incommensurable with some other magnitude C. I say that the remaining one, B, is also incommensurable with C.

**Step 2.** For suppose, if possible, that B is commensurable with C.

**Step 3.** Now A is commensurable with B by hypothesis, and B is commensurable with C by the supposition of Step 2. Thus A and C are each commensurable with the same magnitude B.

**Step 4.** But magnitudes commensurable with the same magnitude are commensurable with one another [10.12]. Therefore A is commensurable with C.

**Step 5.** But A is also, by hypothesis, incommensurable with C. Thus A would be both measured by a common measure with C and yet have no common measure with C, which is impossible by the definition of commensurable and incommensurable magnitudes [D10.1.1].

**Step 6.** Therefore the supposition of Step 2 is false, and B is not commensurable with C; that is, B is incommensurable with C.

**Step 7.** Therefore, if two magnitudes be commensurable, and one of them be incommensurable with any magnitude, the remaining one will also be incommensurable with the same. Q.E.D.

result.statement: If four straight lines be proportional, and the square on the first be greater than the square on the second by the square on a straight line commensurable with the first, the square on the third will also be greater than the square on the fourth by  the square on a straight line commensurable with the third. And, if the square on the first be greater than the square on the second by the square on a straight line incommensurable with the first, the square on the third will also be greater than the square on the fourth by the square on a straight line in-commensurable with the third.
result.proof:
**Step 1.** Let A, B, C, D be four straight lines such that A : B = C : D, and let the square on A be greater than the square on B by the square on a straight line E, so that sq(A) = sq(B) + sq(E).

**Step 2.** Since sq(A) = sq(B) + sq(E), the square on A is greater than the square on B [CN5]; hence A is greater than B, for if A were equal to or less than B, the square on A would be equal to or less than the square on B. Now A : B = C : D and A is greater than B; therefore C is greater than D [5.14].

**Step 3.** Let C be the straight line GK. Bisect GK at L [1.10], and with centre L and distance LG describe the semicircle GHK on GK [P3]. Since D is less than the diameter GK, fit into this circle the straight line GH equal to D, with G as one extremity [4.1], and join HK [P1].

**Step 4.** The angle GHK, being an angle in the semicircle GHK, is right [3.31]. Therefore sq(GK) = sq(GH) + sq(HK) [1.47]. But GK = C and GH = D; hence, writing F for HK, sq(C) = sq(D) + sq(F). Thus the square on C is greater than the square on D by the square on F.

**Step 5.** Since A : B = C : D, and the squares on A, B, C, D are similar rectilineal figures similarly described on these straight lines, sq(A) : sq(B) = sq(C) : sq(D) [6.22].

**Step 6.** Substituting the equalities of Steps 1 and 4, (sq(B) + sq(E)) : sq(B) = (sq(D) + sq(F)) : sq(D).

**Step 7.** These magnitudes are proportional componendo; therefore they are also proportional separando [5.17], so that sq(E) : sq(B) = sq(F) : sq(D).

**Step 8.** The squares on E, B, F, D are similar figures similarly described on these straight lines and are proportional; therefore E : B = F : D [6.22].

**Step 9.** Inversely, B : E = D : F [5.7].

**Step 10.** Since A : B = C : D and B : E = D : F, therefore, ex aequali, A : E = C : F [5.22].

**Step 11.** First case: let E be commensurable with A. Since A : E = C : F and the first, A, is commensurable with the second, E, the third, C, is commensurable with the fourth, F [10.11]. Hence the square on C is greater than the square on D by the square on F, a straight line commensurable with C.

**Step 12.** Second case: let E be incommensurable with A. Since A : E = C : F and the first, A, is incommensurable with the second, E, the third, C, is incommensurable with the fourth, F [10.11]. Hence the square on C is greater than the square on D by the square on F, a straight line incommensurable with C. Q.E.D.

result.statement: If two commensurable magnitudes be added together, the whole will also be commensurable with each of them; and, if the whole be commensurable with one of them, the original magnitudes will also be commensurable.
result.proof:
**Step 1.** Let the two commensurable magnitudes AB, BC be added together, so that the whole is AC. I say first that AC is commensurable with each of AB, BC.

**Step 2.** Since AB, BC are commensurable, they are measured by the same measure [D10.1.1]. Let D be a magnitude which measures both AB and BC.

**Step 3.** Since D measures AB, AB is a multiple of D [D5.2]; let AB be the m-th multiple of D, that is, AB is composed of m magnitudes each equal to D. Likewise, since D measures BC, BC is a multiple of D [D5.2]; let BC be the n-th multiple of D, composed of n magnitudes each equal to D.

**Step 4.** Now AC is AB and BC added together. Since AB is equal to m magnitudes each equal to D, and BC is equal to n magnitudes each equal to D, the whole AC, being the sum of these equals, is equal to m + n magnitudes each equal to D [CN2]. Therefore AC is the (m + n)-th multiple of D, so that D measures AC [D5.2].

**Step 5.** Thus D measures both AB and AC; therefore AB, AC are measured by the same measure, and AB is commensurable with AC [D10.1.1]. Similarly D measures both BC and AC; therefore BC is commensurable with AC [D10.1.1]. Hence the whole AC is commensurable with each of AB, BC.

**Step 6.** Next, let the whole AC be commensurable with one of the original magnitudes, say AB. I say that AB, BC are commensurable.

**Step 7.** Since AC, AB are commensurable, they are measured by the same measure [D10.1.1]. Let D be a magnitude which measures both AC and AB.

**Step 8.** Since D measures AC, AC is a multiple of D [D5.2]; let AC be the k-th multiple of D. Since D measures AB, AB is a multiple of D [D5.2]; let AB be the m-th multiple of D.

**Step 9.** Since AB is a part of the whole AC, AB is less than AC [CN5]; hence the m-th multiple of D is less than the k-th multiple of D, so that m is less than k. Let E be the (k − m)-th multiple of D. Then m magnitudes equal to D together with k − m magnitudes equal to D make k magnitudes equal to D; that is, AB together with E is equal to AC [CN2].

**Step 10.** But AB together with BC is also the whole AC. Therefore AB together with E is equal to AB together with BC. Subtracting the common magnitude AB from each, the remainders are equal [CN3]; therefore BC is equal to E, the (k − m)-th multiple of D. Hence BC is a multiple of D, and D measures BC [D5.2].

**Step 11.** Thus D measures both AB and BC; therefore AB, BC are measured by the same measure, and AB is commensurable with BC [D10.1.1]. If instead AC were commensurable with BC, the same argument with the roles of AB and BC interchanged shows that BC, AB are commensurable.

**Step 12.** Therefore, if two commensurable magnitudes be added together, the whole is commensurable with each of them; and, if the whole be commensurable with one of them, the original magnitudes are commensurable. Q.E.D.

result.statement: If two incommensurable magnitudes be added together, the whole will also be incommensurable with each of them; and, if the whole be incommensurable with one of them, the original magnitudes will also be incommensurable.
result.proof:
## Proposition 10.16
**Statement:** If two incommensurable magnitudes be added together, the whole will also be incommensurable with each of them; and, if the whole be incommensurable with one of them, the original magnitudes will also be incommensurable.

**Step 1.** Let AB, BC be two incommensurable magnitudes, and let them be added together so that they make up the whole AC. By D10.1.1, to say AB, BC are incommensurable means that AB, BC cannot have any common measure.

**Step 2.** I say first that the whole AC is incommensurable with AB. For suppose, if possible, that AC is commensurable with AB.

**Step 3.** Then the whole AC is commensurable with one of the two magnitudes AB, BC of which it is composed; therefore, by the second part of 10.15, the original magnitudes AB, BC are commensurable, that is (D10.1.1), some one magnitude measures both AB and BC.

**Step 4.** But by hypothesis (Step 1) AB, BC are incommensurable, so that by D10.1.1 they cannot have any common measure. Thus the same two magnitudes AB, BC both have and cannot have a common measure: which is impossible.

**Step 5.** Therefore AC is not commensurable with AB; that is, no one magnitude measures both AC and AB, so by D10.1.1 AC is incommensurable with AB.

**Step 6.** Similarly, suppose, if possible, that AC is commensurable with BC. Then again the whole AC is commensurable with one of AB, BC, so by the second part of 10.15 AB, BC are commensurable, which by D10.1.1 contradicts the hypothesis that AB, BC are incommensurable. Therefore AC is incommensurable with BC also.

**Step 7.** Hence, if two incommensurable magnitudes AB, BC be added together, the whole AC is incommensurable with each of them, which is the first part of the proposition.

**Step 8.** Next, let the whole AC be incommensurable with one of the magnitudes AB, BC of which it is composed; say AC is incommensurable with AB, so that by D10.1.1 AC and AB cannot have any common measure. I say that AB, BC are incommensurable.

**Step 9.** For suppose, if possible, that AB, BC are commensurable.

**Step 10.** Then AB, BC are two commensurable magnitudes added together making the whole AC; therefore, by the first part of 10.15, the whole AC is commensurable with each of AB, BC, and in particular AC is commensurable with AB, that is (D10.1.1), some one magnitude measures both AC and AB.

**Step 11.** But by hypothesis (Step 8) AC and AB cannot have any common measure (D10.1.1). Thus AC, AB both have and cannot have a common measure: which is impossible.

**Step 12.** Therefore AB, BC are not commensurable; that is, no one magnitude measures both of them, so by D10.1.1 AB, BC are incommensurable. The argument is the same if it is BC, rather than AB, with which the whole AC is incommensurable: supposing AB, BC commensurable, 10.15 would make AC commensurable with BC, contrary to hypothesis.

**Step 13.** Hence, if the whole be incommensurable with one of the two magnitudes, the original magnitudes are incommensurable, which is the second part of the proposition. Therefore, if two incommensurable magnitudes be added together, the whole is incommensurable with each of them; and if the whole be incommensurable with one of them, the original magnitudes are incommensurable. Q.E.D.

*Path note:* Each part of 10.16 is the contrapositive of the corresponding part of 10.15, so the most direct route is the reductio through 10.15, with D10.1.1 supplying the equivalence between "not commensurable" and "incommensurable". The alternative route, exhibiting a common measure D of the whole and one part and observing that D then measures the remainder, reproduces the interior of 10.15's own proof and was therefore not taken.

**USED:** D10.1.1, 10.15

result.statement: If there be two unequal straight lines, and to the greater there be applied a parallelogram equal to the fourth part of the square on the less and deficient by a square figure, and if it divide it into parts which are commensurable in length, then the square on the greater will be greater than the square on the less by the square on a straight line commensurable with the greater. And, if the square on the greater be greater than the square on the less by the square on a straight line commensurable with  the greater, and if there be applied to the greater a parallelogram equal to the fourth part of the square on the less and deficient by a square figure, it will divide it into parts which are commensurable in length.
result.proof:
**Step 1.** Let A, BC be the two unequal straight lines, BC being the greater. Write sq(X) for the square on X and rect(X, Y) for the rectangle contained by X, Y. Let the parallelogram applied to BC, equal to the fourth part of sq(A) and deficient by a square figure, be rect(BD, DC), the deficient square being the square on DC. Thus four times rect(BD, DC) is equal to sq(A).

**Step 2.** Bisect BC at E [1.10]. Since BC is cut at E, sq(BC) = sq(BE) + sq(EC) + 2 rect(BE, EC) [2.4]; and BE = EC, so sq(BE) = sq(EC) and rect(BE, EC) = sq(EC). Hence sq(BC) is four times sq(EC).

**Step 3.** D does not coincide with E, so BD, DC are unequal. For if D were E, rect(BD, DC) would be rect(BE, EC) = sq(EC); then four times rect(BD, DC), which is sq(A) (Step 1), would equal four times sq(EC), which is sq(BC) (Step 2); so sq(A) = sq(BC) [CN1]. But A is less than BC, so that sq(A) is less than sq(BC), sq(A) being equal to the square on a part of BC cut off equal to A [1.3], which is a part of sq(BC) [CN5]. This is impossible.

**Step 4.** Let BD be the greater of BD, DC; this is no restriction, since all the hypotheses are symmetric in B and C. Then D lies between E and C: for if D lay between B and E, we should have BD < BE = EC < DC [CN5], contrary to BD > DC. Consequently ED is a part of EC, so that ED < EC = BE [CN5].

**Step 5.** From EB, which is greater than ED, cut off EF equal to ED [1.3]; F lies between B and E. Since BE = EC and EF = ED, the remainders are equal: BF = DC [CN3]. Further, DF = DE + EF is double of DE. Hence BD = BF + FD = DC + DF, and BC = BF + FD + DC; that is, BC is composed of DF and the sum BF + DC, which is double of DC.

**Step 6.** Since BC is cut into equal segments at E and into unequal segments at D, rect(BD, DC) + sq(ED) = sq(EC) [2.5]. Adding this equation to itself, and the result again to itself, four times rect(BD, DC) together with four times sq(ED) is equal to four times sq(EC) [CN2].

**Step 7.** Now four times rect(BD, DC) = sq(A) (Step 1) and four times sq(EC) = sq(BC) (Step 2). Also, DF being cut at E with DE = EF, sq(DF) = sq(DE) + sq(EF) + 2 rect(DE, EF) = four times sq(DE) [2.4]. Substituting these in Step 6, sq(A) + sq(DF) = sq(BC) [CN1]. Therefore the square on BC is greater than the square on A by the square on DF.

**Step 8.** [First part.] Suppose BD, DC are commensurable in length. Since BD = DC + DF (Step 5) and the whole BD is commensurable with the one part DC, the parts DC and DF are commensurable [10.15]. Again, BD, DC being commensurable, their sum BC is commensurable with DC [10.15]. So DF and BC are each commensurable with DC, hence they are commensurable with one another [10.12]. Thus DF is commensurable in length with BC, and by Step 7 the square on the greater BC is greater than the square on the less A by the square on DF, a straight line commensurable in length with BC. This proves the first part.

**Step 9.** [Converse.] Suppose now that sq(BC) is greater than sq(A) by sq(G), where G is commensurable in length with BC, and that the parallelogram equal to the fourth part of sq(A) and deficient by a square figure is applied to BC as rect(BD, DC). Make the same construction (Steps 2–5). By Step 7, sq(BC) is greater than sq(A) by sq(DF). Hence sq(DF) = sq(G), each being the excess of sq(BC) over sq(A) [CN3]; whence DF = G, for if DF and G were unequal the square on the less would be a part of, and so less than, the square on the greater [CN5]. Therefore DF is commensurable in length with BC.

**Step 10.** Since BC is composed of DF and BF + DC (Step 5), and the whole BC is commensurable with the part DF, the parts DF and BF + DC are commensurable [10.15]. But BF + DC is double of DC, so that DC measures both DC and BF + DC, and DC is commensurable with BF + DC [D10.1.1]. Thus DF and DC are each commensurable with BF + DC, hence they are commensurable with one another [10.12].

**Step 11.** Since DC, DF are commensurable, their sum BD = DC + DF (Step 5) is commensurable with DC [10.15]. Therefore the applied parallelogram rect(BD, DC) divides BC into parts BD, DC which are commensurable in length. This proves the converse.

result.statement: If there be two unequal straight lines, and to the greater there be applied a parallelogram equal to the fourth part of the square on the less and deficient by a square figure, and if it divide it into parts which are incommensurable, the square on the greater will be greater than the square on the less by the square on a straight line incommensurable with the greater. And, if the square on the greater be greater than the square on the less by the square on a straight line incommensurable with the greater, and if there be applied to the greater a parallelogram equal to the fourth part of the square on the less and deficient by a square figure, it divides it into parts which are incommensurable. Let A, BC be two unequal straight lines, of which BC is the greater, and to BC let there be applied a parallelogram equal to the fourth part of the square on the less, A, and deficient by a square figure.
result.proof:
## Proposition 10.18
**Statement:** If there be two unequal straight lines, and to the greater there be applied a parallelogram equal to the fourth part of the square on the less and deficient by a square figure, and if it divide it into parts which are incommensurable, the square on the greater will be greater than the square on the less by the square on a straight line incommensurable with the greater. And, if the square on the greater be greater than the square on the less by the square on a straight line incommensurable with the greater, and if there be applied to the greater a parallelogram equal to the fourth part of the square on the less and deficient by a square figure, it divides it into parts which are incommensurable.

Let A, BC be the two unequal straight lines, BC the greater, and let the parallelogram applied to BC, equal to the fourth part of the square on A and deficient by a square figure, be the rectangle contained by BD, DC, where D is the point of BC at which the parallelogram divides it and the deficiency is the square on DC. Thus the rectangle BD, DC is the fourth part of the square on A, i.e. the square on A is four times the rectangle BD, DC. The parts of BC are BD, DC.

First part: BD, DC are incommensurable in length; to prove that the square on BC exceeds the square on A by the square on a straight line incommensurable in length with BC. Second part (converse): the square on BC exceeds the square on A by the square on a straight line incommensurable in length with BC; to prove that BD, DC are incommensurable in length.

**Step 1.** Bisect BC at E [1.10], so that BE = EC and BC is double EC. Since BC is cut at E, the square on BC is equal to the squares on BE, EC together with twice the rectangle BE, EC [2.4]; and because BE = EC, the square on BE and the rectangle BE, EC (being contained by two straight lines equal to EC) are each equal to the square on EC. Hence the square on BC is four times the square on EC.

**Step 2.** The point D does not coincide with E. In the first part: if D were E, then BD = DC, and either of them would measure both, so BD, DC would be commensurable [D10.1.1], contrary to hypothesis. In the second part: if D were E, then each of BD, DC would be equal to EC, so the rectangle BD, DC would be the square on EC, which is the fourth part of the square on BC (Step 1); then the square on A, being four times the rectangle BD, DC, would be equal to the square on BC [CN1]. But by hypothesis the square on BC is the square on A together with a square, and so is greater than the square on A [CN5]. Contradiction.

**Step 3.** Therefore D lies between E and one of the extremities of BC. The hypotheses and conclusions are symmetrical in the two parts BD, DC, so we may name the extremities so that D lies between E and C. Then ED is a part of EC, so ED is less than EC, i.e. less than EB [CN5]. From EB cut off EF equal to ED [1.3]; F lies between E and B, so the points lie on BC in the order B, F, E, D, C.

**Step 4.** Since BE = EC and EF = ED, subtracting equals from equals gives BF = DC [CN3]. Further FD is made up of FE, ED with FE = ED, so FD is double ED; and BC is made up of BF, FD, DC, so that BC = (BF + DC) + FD.

**Step 5.** BC is cut into equal segments at E and into unequal segments at D; therefore the rectangle BD, DC together with the square on ED is equal to the square on EC [2.5]. Adding equals to equals three times over, four times the rectangle BD, DC together with four times the square on ED is equal to four times the square on EC [CN2].

**Step 6.** FD is cut at E, so the square on FD is equal to the squares on FE, ED together with twice the rectangle FE, ED [2.4]; and since FE = ED, the square on FE and the rectangle FE, ED are each equal to the square on ED. Hence the square on FD is four times the square on ED.

**Step 7.** Now the square on A is four times the rectangle BD, DC (hypothesis), the square on FD is four times the square on ED (Step 6), and the square on BC is four times the square on EC (Step 1). Adding the first two, the squares on A, FD together are equal to four times the rectangle BD, DC together with four times the square on ED [CN2], which is equal to four times the square on EC (Step 5), that is, to the square on BC. Therefore the squares on A, FD together are equal to the square on BC [CN1]: the square on BC is greater than the square on A by the square on FD. This holds under the hypothesis of either part; it remains to compare FD with BC.

**Step 8.** (First part.) BD, DC are incommensurable in length and added together make BC; therefore the whole BC is incommensurable in length with DC [10.16].

**Step 9.** Since BF = DC (Step 4), the sum BF + DC is double DC; thus DC measures BF + DC (twice) and measures itself, so DC and BF + DC are measured by the same measure and are commensurable in length [D10.1.1].

**Step 10.** DC and BF + DC are commensurable, and DC is incommensurable with BC (Step 8); therefore BF + DC is incommensurable in length with BC [10.13].

**Step 11.** BC = (BF + DC) + FD (Step 4), and the whole BC is incommensurable with the one part BF + DC; therefore BF + DC and FD are incommensurable [10.16]; and since these two incommensurable magnitudes added together make BC, the whole BC is incommensurable in length with FD [10.16]. Hence, by Step 7, the square on BC is greater than the square on A by the square on FD, a straight line incommensurable in length with BC. This proves the first part.

**Step 12.** (Second part.) Let the square on BC be greater than the square on A by the square on G, where G is incommensurable in length with BC; so the square on BC is equal to the squares on A, G together. By Step 7 the square on BC is equal to the squares on A, FD together. Subtracting the square on A from each, the square on G is equal to the square on FD [CN3]. Hence G = FD; for if G, FD were unequal, the square on the less, placed within the square on the greater with a common angle, would be a part of it and so less than it [CN5]. Therefore any common measure of FD and BC would be a common measure of G and BC, which have none; so FD is incommensurable in length with BC [D10.1.1].

**Step 13.** BC = (BF + DC) + FD (Step 4), and the whole BC is incommensurable with the one part FD; therefore BF + DC and FD are incommensurable [10.16]; and since these incommensurable magnitudes added together make BC, the whole BC is incommensurable in length with BF + DC [10.16].

**Step 14.** BF + DC and DC are commensurable (Step 9), and BF + DC is incommensurable with BC (Step 13); therefore DC is incommensurable in length with BC [10.13].

**Step 15.** BD, DC added together make BC, and the whole BC is incommensurable with the one part DC; therefore BD, DC are incommensurable in length [10.16]. Thus the applied parallelogram divides BC into incommensurable parts. This proves the second part.

result.statement: The rectangle contained by rational straight lines commensurable in length is rational.
result.proof:
**Step 1.** Let ρ be the assigned rational straight line (D10.1.3). Let AB, BC be rational straight lines commensurable in length, placed so that the angle ABC is right, and let AC be the rectangle contained by AB, BC, that is, the rectangular parallelogram whose sides about the right angle at B are AB and BC (D2.1). I say that the rectangle AC is rational.

**Step 2.** On AB describe the square AD (1.46), and let D be the vertex of the square adjacent to B, so that BD is a side of the square. Since a square is equilateral and right-angled (D1.22), BD is equal to AB and the angle ABD is right.

**Step 3.** Since AB is rational, by D10.1.3 it is commensurable with ρ, whether in length and in square or in square only; in either case AB is commensurable in square with ρ. Therefore, by D10.1.2, the square on AB and the square on ρ are measured by the same area, that is, they are commensurable (D10.1.1). Hence the square AD, being the square on AB, is commensurable with the square on ρ, and is therefore rational (D10.1.4).

**Step 4.** Since AB and BC are commensurable in length, some magnitude measures both AB and BC (D10.1.1). But BD is equal to AB (Step 2); therefore the same magnitude measures BD also. Thus BD and BC are measured by the same measure, so BD is commensurable in length with BC (D10.1.1).

**Step 5.** The square AD and the rectangle AC are parallelograms standing on the bases BD and BC respectively, and both are under the same height AB: for the angle ABD is right (Step 2) and the angle ABC is right (Step 1), so that AB is the perpendicular drawn from the vertex A to each base (D6.4). Therefore, by 6.1, as BD is to BC, so is the square AD to the rectangle AC.

**Step 6.** In this proportion the first term BD is commensurable with the second term BC (Step 4). Therefore, by 10.11, the third term, the square AD, is commensurable with the fourth term, the rectangle AC.

**Step 7.** Now the square AD is rational (Step 3), that is, it is commensurable with the square on ρ (D10.1.4); and the rectangle AC is commensurable with the square AD (Step 6). Hence the rectangle AC and the square on ρ are each commensurable with the same magnitude, the square AD; therefore, by 10.12, the rectangle AC is commensurable with the square on ρ.

**Step 8.** But areas commensurable with the square on the assigned rational straight line are rational (D10.1.4). Therefore the rectangle AC contained by the rational straight lines AB, BC commensurable in length is rational. Q.E.D.

result.statement: If a rational area be applied to a rational straight line, it produces as breadth a straight line rational and commensurable in length with the straight line to which it is applied.
result.proof:
**Step 1.** Let the rational area AB be applied to the rational straight line AC, producing CB as breadth; that is, AB is the rectangle contained by AC, CB, so that CB stands at right angles to AC at the point C (D2.1). Let the assigned straight line in respect of which straight lines and areas are called rational be denoted ρ (D10.1.3, D10.1.4). I say that CB is rational and commensurable in length with CA.

**Step 2.** On AC describe the square AD (1.46), placing it on the side of AC opposite to the rectangle AB, and let its side through C be CD. Since AD is a square, CD is at right angles to AC (D1.22); and CB is also at right angles to AC (Step 1), the two lines CD, CB lying on opposite sides of AC. Hence the adjacent angles ACD, ACB are together equal to two right angles, so that DC is in a straight line with CB (1.14). Thus the square AD and the rectangle AB have their bases DC, CB lying in the one straight line DB.

**Step 3.** Preliminary remark: if two straight lines are commensurable in length, the squares on them are commensurable. For the squares on straight lines commensurable in length have to one another the ratio which a square number has to a square number (10.9), and magnitudes which have to one another the ratio which a number has to a number are commensurable (10.6).

**Step 4.** The square AD is rational. For AC, being rational, is commensurable with ρ either in length, and then also in square by Step 3, or in square only (D10.1.3); in either case the square on AC is commensurable with the square on ρ (D10.1.2), that is, the square AD is rational (D10.1.4).

**Step 5.** The area AB is rational by hypothesis. Therefore AD and AB are each commensurable with the square on ρ (D10.1.4); and magnitudes commensurable with the same magnitude are commensurable with one another, so that AD is commensurable with AB (10.12).

**Step 6.** The parallelograms AD, AB have their bases DC, CB in the one straight line DB (Step 2) and are under the same height, namely AC, which is perpendicular to DB at C and joins the base line to the opposite sides of both figures. Therefore, as the square AD is to the rectangle AB, so is DC to CB (6.1).

**Step 7.** Since the four magnitudes AD, AB, DC, CB are proportional (Step 6) and the first, AD, is commensurable with the second, AB (Step 5), the third, DC, is commensurable with the fourth, CB (10.11).

**Step 8.** But DC is equal to CA, both being sides of the square AD (D1.22). Hence the magnitude which is a common measure of DC and CB measures CA also, so that CB is commensurable in length with CA (D10.1.1).

**Step 9.** Since CB is commensurable in length with CA, the square on CB is commensurable with the square on CA (Step 3); and the square on CA is commensurable with the square on ρ (Step 4). Therefore the square on CB is commensurable with the square on ρ (10.12); that is, CB is commensurable in square with ρ (D10.1.2), and hence CB is rational (D10.1.3).

**Step 10.** Therefore the breadth CB produced by applying the rational area AB to the rational straight line AC is rational and commensurable in length with CA, the straight line to which the area was applied. Q.E.D.

result.statement: The rectangle contained by rational straight lines commensurable in square only is irrational, and the side of the square equal to it is irrational. Let the latter be called medial.
result.proof:
**Step 1.** Let AB, BC be rational straight lines commensurable in square only (D10.1.3, D10.1.2), and let AC be the rectangle contained by AB, BC (D2.1), so that the angle ABC is right. I say that the rectangle AC is irrational, and that the side of the square equal to AC is irrational.

**Step 2.** On AB describe the square AD (1.46), placing it on the side of AB remote from C; let its vertices be A, B, D, E. Since AD is a square, BD is equal to AB and the angle ABD is right (D1.22).

**Step 3.** With the straight line AB, at the point B on it, the two straight lines BD, BC lie on opposite sides of AB and make the adjacent angles ABD, ABC, each of which is right; hence these adjacent angles are together equal to two right angles. Therefore DB is in a straight line with BC (1.14), and D, B, C lie on one straight line DC.

**Step 4.** The square AD is rational. For AB is rational, that is, it is commensurable with the assigned rational straight line, whether in length and in square or in square only (D10.1.3); in either case AB is commensurable in square with the assigned straight line, so that the square on AB and the square on the assigned straight line are measured by the same area (D10.1.2), i.e. they are commensurable. But the square on the assigned straight line is rational, and areas commensurable with it are rational (D10.1.4). Therefore the square AD, being the square on AB, is rational.

**Step 5.** Since AB, BC are commensurable in square only, they are not commensurable in length, so that AB and BC have no common measure (D10.1.1). And BD is equal to AB (Step 2); hence any magnitude measuring both DB and BC would measure both AB and BC. Therefore DB is incommensurable in length with BC (D10.1.1).

**Step 6.** The square AD and the rectangle AC are parallelograms whose bases DB, BC lie on the one straight line DC (Step 3), and each has the same height, namely the perpendicular AB drawn from the common vertex A to the base (D6.4), since the angles ABD, ABC are right. Therefore, as DB is to BC, so is the square AD to the rectangle AC (6.1).

**Step 7.** Thus the four magnitudes DB, BC, AD, AC are proportional, and the first, DB, is incommensurable with the second, BC (Step 5). Therefore the third, the square AD, is incommensurable with the fourth, the rectangle AC (10.11).

**Step 8.** Now the square AD is rational (Step 4); that is, AD and the square on the assigned rational straight line are two commensurable magnitudes, and one of them, AD, is incommensurable with the magnitude AC (Step 7). Therefore the remaining one, the square on the assigned straight line, is also incommensurable with AC (10.13). But areas incommensurable with the square on the assigned straight line are irrational (D10.1.4). Therefore the rectangle AC is irrational.

**Step 9.** Let a square be constructed equal to the rectangle AC (2.14), and let G be its side. The rectangle AC is not itself a square but another rectilineal figure, and it is irrational; therefore the straight line G, on which is described a square equal to AC, is irrational (D10.1.4).

**Step 10.** Therefore the rectangle contained by rational straight lines commensurable in square only is irrational, and the side of the square equal to it is irrational. Let the latter be called medial. Q.E.D.

result.statement: The square on a medial straight line, if applied to a rational straight line, produces as breadth a straight line rational and incommensurable in length with that to which it is applied.
result.proof:
## Proposition 10.22
**Statement:** The square on a medial straight line, if applied to a rational straight line, produces as breadth a straight line rational and incommensurable in length with that to which it is applied.

**Step 1.** Let A be a medial straight line and CB a rational straight line, "rational" and "medial" being understood throughout with reference to one assigned rational straight line H [D10.1.3]. To CB let there be applied, in a right angle, the parallelogram BD equal to the square on A, so that CD is its breadth [1.44, 1.45]. BD is thus a rectangle, namely the rectangle contained by DC, CB [D2.1]. I say that CD is rational and incommensurable in length with CB.

**Step 2.** Since A is medial, the square on A is equal to a rectangle contained by two rational straight lines commensurable in square only [10.21]. Let the square on A be equal to the rectangle GF contained by GE, EF [D2.1], where GE, EF are rational and commensurable in square only.

**Step 3.** Each of BD, GF is equal to the square on A; therefore BD is equal to GF [CN1]. Both BD and GF are right-angled, and all right angles are equal to one another [P4]; hence BD and GF are equal and equiangular parallelograms. In equal and equiangular parallelograms the sides about the equal angles are reciprocally proportional [6.14]; therefore, as CB is to EG, so is EF to CD.

**Step 4.** Since the four straight lines CB, EG, EF, CD are proportional, the squares on them, being similar rectilineal figures similarly described on them, are also proportional [6.22]: as the square on CB is to the square on EG, so is the square on EF to the square on CD.

**Step 5.** CB is rational, so it is commensurable with H either in length or in square only [D10.1.3]; in either case the square on CB is measured by a common area with the square on H, that is, the square on CB is commensurable with the square on H and is rational [D10.1.2, D10.1.4]. In the same way the square on EG is commensurable with the square on H. Magnitudes commensurable with the same magnitude are commensurable with one another [10.12]; therefore the square on CB is commensurable with the square on EG.

**Step 6.** In the proportion of Step 4 the first magnitude, the square on CB, is commensurable with the second, the square on EG; therefore the third, the square on EF, is commensurable with the fourth, the square on CD [10.11].

**Step 7.** EF is rational, so, exactly as in Step 5, the square on EF is commensurable with the square on H [D10.1.3, D10.1.2, D10.1.4]. The square on CD is commensurable with the square on EF (Step 6), and the square on EF is commensurable with the square on H; therefore the square on CD is commensurable with the square on H [10.12]. Hence the square on CD is rational [D10.1.4], CD is commensurable in square with H [D10.1.2], and therefore CD is rational [D10.1.3].

**Step 8.** Since EF, EG are commensurable in square only, EF is incommensurable in length with EG [D10.1.1, D10.1.2]. Place EF, EG in a straight line and consider the square on EF and the rectangle contained by FE, EG: these are parallelograms under the same height EF, with bases EF and EG respectively, and parallelograms under the same height are to one another as their bases [6.1]. Therefore, as EF is to EG, so is the square on EF to the rectangle FE, EG. Since the first, EF, is incommensurable with the second, EG, the third, the square on EF, is incommensurable with the fourth, the rectangle FE, EG [10.11].

**Step 9.** The square on CD is commensurable with the square on EF (Step 6), and the square on EF is incommensurable with the rectangle FE, EG (Step 8); therefore the square on CD is incommensurable with the rectangle FE, EG [10.13]. But the rectangle FE, EG is GF, which equals the square on A, which equals BD, the rectangle DC, CB; hence the rectangle FE, EG is equal to the rectangle DC, CB [CN1], and equal magnitudes are commensurable with one another, since any magnitude measuring the one measures the other [D10.1.1]. Therefore, the rectangle DC, CB being commensurable with the rectangle FE, EG, which is incommensurable with the square on CD, the square on CD is incommensurable with the rectangle DC, CB [10.13].

**Step 10.** The square on CD and the rectangle contained by DC, CB are parallelograms under the same height CD, with bases CD and CB respectively; therefore, as the square on CD is to the rectangle DC, CB, so is CD to CB [6.1]. Since the first, the square on CD, is incommensurable with the second, the rectangle DC, CB, the third, CD, is incommensurable with the fourth, CB [10.11]; that is, CD is incommensurable in length with CB [D10.1.1].

**Step 11.** Therefore CD is rational (Step 7) and incommensurable in length with CB (Step 10). Hence the square on a medial straight line, applied to a rational straight line, produces as breadth a straight line rational and incommensurable in length with that to which it is applied. Q.E.D.

*Path note.* The fact "as EF is to EG, so is the square on EF to the rectangle FE, EG" (used in Steps 8 and 10) is Euclid's lemma following 10.21; since lemmas are not separately citable, it is derived directly from 6.1, from which that lemma itself follows. For Step 4, 6.22 was chosen over the route through duplicate ratio (D5.9 with 6.20 corollary) as the more direct.
