result.statement: A straight line commensurable with a medial straight line is medial.
result.proof:
**Statement:** A straight line commensurable with a medial straight line is medial.

Let A be a medial straight line, and let B be a straight line commensurable with A (whether in length, or in square only). I say that B is medial.

**Step 1.** Set out a rational straight line CD [D10.1.3]. Describe the squares on A and on B [1.46]. To CD apply the rectangle CE, in a right angle, equal to the square on A, producing DE as breadth; and again to CD apply the rectangle CF, in a right angle, equal to the square on B, producing DF as breadth [1.45]. Since both rectangles have CD as a side and their other sides stand at right angles to CD at D, the breadths DE, DF lie along the one straight line drawn through D at right angles to CD. Thus CE is the rectangle contained by CD, DE, and CF is the rectangle contained by CD, DF [D2.1].

**Step 2.** Since A is medial, and CE, the square on A, has been applied to the rational straight line CD, the breadth DE is rational and incommensurable in length with CD [10.22].

**Step 3.** Since A is commensurable with B, the square on A is commensurable with the square on B. For if A, B are commensurable in square only, their squares are measured by the same area [D10.1.2]; and if A, B are commensurable in length, the square on A has to the square on B the ratio which a square number has to a square number [10.9], so that the square on A is commensurable with the square on B [10.6]. In either case the square on A is commensurable with the square on B.

**Step 4.** But CE is equal to the square on A, and CF is equal to the square on B; hence any area which measures the square on A measures CE, and any area which measures the square on B measures CF. Therefore CE is commensurable with CF [D10.1.1].

**Step 5.** Now CE, CF are parallelograms under the same height CD; therefore, as CE is to CF, so is DE to DF [6.1].

**Step 6.** And CE is commensurable with CF; therefore DE is also commensurable with DF [10.11], that is, DE is commensurable in length with DF.

**Step 7.** Since DE, DF are commensurable in length, the square on DE has to the square on DF the ratio which a square number has to a square number [10.9]; therefore the square on DE is commensurable with the square on DF [10.6]. But DE is rational, and it is incommensurable in length with CD [Step 2]; therefore DE is commensurable in square with CD [D10.1.3], that is, the square on DE is commensurable with the square on CD [D10.1.2]. Now the square on DF is commensurable with the square on DE, and the square on DE is commensurable with the square on CD; therefore the square on DF is commensurable with the square on CD [10.12]. Hence DF is commensurable in square with CD, and therefore DF is rational [D10.1.3].

**Step 8.** Again, DE is commensurable with DF, and DE is incommensurable in length with CD; therefore DF is also incommensurable in length with CD [10.13].

**Step 9.** Therefore CD, DF are rational straight lines commensurable in square only. Hence the rectangle contained by CD, DF, that is, CF, is irrational, and the side of the square equal to CF is medial [10.21].

**Step 10.** But the square on B is equal to CF; therefore B is the side of the square equal to the rectangle CF, which is contained by rational straight lines commensurable in square only. Therefore B is medial [10.21].

Therefore a straight line commensurable with a medial straight line is medial. Q.E.D.

**USED:** D2.1, D10.1.1, D10.1.2, D10.1.3, 1.45, 1.46, 6.1, 10.6, 10.9, 10.11, 10.12, 10.13, 10.21, 10.22

result.statement: The rectangle contained by medial straight lines commensurable in length is medial.
result.proof:
**Step 1.** Let AB, BC be medial straight lines commensurable in length, placed so as to contain a right angle at B, and let AC be the rectangle contained by AB, BC. It is to be proved that the rectangle AC is medial.

**Step 2.** On AB describe the square AD [1.46], placing it so that its side BD lies along the straight line CB produced beyond B. Since AD is a square, its side DB is equal to AB [1.46].

**Step 3.** Since AB is medial, the square AD on AB is a medial area; for, by the definition of a medial straight line, the square on it is equal to a rectangle contained by rational straight lines commensurable in square only, and such an area is what is called medial [10.21].

**Step 4.** The square AD and the rectangle AC are parallelograms under the same height, namely AB, standing on the bases DB, BC, which lie in the one straight line DC; therefore, as DB is to BC, so is AD to AC [6.1]. And since DB is equal to AB, as DB is to BC, so is AB to BC [5.7]; hence, as AB is to BC, so is AD to AC.

**Step 5.** Now AB is commensurable in length with BC. Therefore, the four magnitudes AB, BC, AD, AC being proportional and the first commensurable with the second, the third AD is commensurable with the fourth AC [10.11].

**Step 6.** But AD is a medial area [Step 3], and an area commensurable with a medial area is medial [10.23, Porism]. Therefore AC is medial.

**Step 7.** Therefore the rectangle AC, contained by the medial straight lines AB, BC which are commensurable in length, is medial. Q.E.D.

result.statement: The rectangle contained by medial straight lines commensurable in square only is either rational or medial.
result.proof:
## Proposition 10.25
**Statement:** The rectangle contained by medial straight lines commensurable in square only is either rational or medial.

**Step 1.** Let AB, BC be medial straight lines commensurable in square only, and let AC be the rectangle contained by them, so that the angle ABC is right. I say that AC is either rational or medial.

**Step 2.** On AB and BC describe the squares AD and BE [1.46], placing AD so that its side BD lies on CB produced, and BE so that its side BO lies on AB produced; thus DB = BA and BO = BC.

**Step 3.** Set out a rational straight line FG [D10.1.3]. To FG apply, in a right angle, the rectangle GH equal to AD, producing FH as breadth; to HM apply the rectangle MK equal to AC, producing HK as breadth; to KN apply the rectangle NL equal to BE, producing KL as breadth [1.44, 1.45]. Since the angles FHM, MHK are right, FH and HK are in a straight line, and likewise HK and KL [1.14]; and since GH, MK are parallelograms, HM = FG and KN = HM = FG [1.34], so that HM and KN are rational straight lines.

**Step 4.** GH is equal to the square AD on the medial straight line AB and is applied to the rational straight line FG; therefore FH is rational and incommensurable in length with FG [10.22]. Likewise NL is equal to the square BE on the medial straight line BC and is applied to the rational straight line KN; therefore KL is rational and incommensurable in length with KN, that is, with FG [10.22].

**Step 5.** Since AB, BC are commensurable in square, the squares AD, BE on them are measured by the same area, i.e. AD is commensurable with BE [D10.1.2, D10.1.1]. GH = AD and NL = BE; hence GH is commensurable with NL. But GH, NL are parallelograms under the same height (between the parallels FL, GO) on the bases FH, KL, so that GH : NL = FH : KL [6.1]. Therefore FH is commensurable in length with KL [10.11].

**Step 6.** FH and KL are rational straight lines commensurable in length; therefore the rectangle contained by FH, KL is rational [10.19].

**Step 7.** Since DB = BA, DB : BC = AB : BC; and since BO = BC, AB : BC = AB : BO [5.7]. Therefore DB : BC = AB : BO [5.11]. But AD and AC are parallelograms under the same height BA on the bases DB, BC, so AD : AC = DB : BC; and AC and BE are parallelograms under the same height BC on the bases AB, BO, so AC : BE = AB : BO [6.1]. Therefore AD : AC = AC : BE [5.11].

**Step 8.** GH = AD, MK = AC and NL = BE; therefore GH : MK = MK : NL [5.7, 5.11]. But GH : MK = FH : HK and MK : NL = HK : KL, these being parallelograms under the same height on the bases FH, HK, KL [6.1]. Therefore FH : HK = HK : KL [5.11].

**Step 9.** FH, HK, KL are thus three proportional straight lines; therefore the rectangle contained by FH, KL is equal to the square on HK [6.17]. But the rectangle FH, KL is rational (Step 6), that is, commensurable with the square on the assigned rational straight line; the square on HK, being equal to it, is measured by the same measure and so is also rational [D10.1.1, D10.1.4]. Hence HK is commensurable in square with the assigned rational straight line, and HK is rational [D10.1.2, D10.1.3].

**Step 10.** The rectangle HN (that is, MK) is contained by HM and HK, both rational straight lines (Steps 3, 9). Now HK is either commensurable in length with HM or incommensurable in length with it [D10.1.1].
(a) If HK is commensurable in length with HM, HN is the rectangle contained by rational straight lines commensurable in length; therefore HN is rational [10.19].
(b) If HK is incommensurable in length with HM: the squares on HK and on HM are each commensurable with the square on the assigned rational straight line [D10.1.3, D10.1.4], hence commensurable with one another [10.12], so that HK, HM are commensurable in square [D10.1.2]; being also incommensurable in length, they are rational straight lines commensurable in square only, and therefore the rectangle HN contained by them is medial [10.21].

**Step 11.** Therefore HN is either rational or medial. But HN = MK = AC; therefore AC, the rectangle contained by the medial straight lines AB, BC commensurable in square only, is either rational or medial. Q.E.D.

Remark: only the commensurability in square of AB, BC (Step 5) was used; their incommensurability in length plays no part in the argument, and which alternative of Step 10 obtains depends on whether HK is commensurable in length with HM.

result.statement: A medial area does not exceed a medial area by a rational area.
result.proof:
**Step 1.** Terms. A medial straight line is the side of the square equal to the rectangle contained by two rational straight lines commensurable in square only (10.21); a medial area is an area equal to the square on a medial straight line. A rational area is an area commensurable with the square on the rational straight line set out (D10.1.4).

**Step 2.** Suppose, if possible, that the medial area AB exceeds the medial area AC by the rational area DB; that is, AB is greater than AC, and DB is the excess of AB over AC, so that AB is equal to AC together with DB.

**Step 3.** Set out a rational straight line EF (D10.1.3). To EF apply, in a right angle, the rectangle FH equal to AB, producing EH as breadth (1.44, 1.45); thus FH is the rectangle contained by EF, EH.

**Step 4.** Likewise apply to EF, in a right angle and on the same side, the rectangle FG equal to AC, producing EG as breadth, EG lying along EH from E (1.44, 1.45). Since AC is less than AB, EG is less than EH; for if EG were not less than EH, the rectangle FG would contain the rectangle FH and so would not be less than it (CN5), that is, AC would not be less than AB. Hence G lies on EH between E and H.

**Step 5.** Since EH is cut at G, the rectangle contained by EF, EH is equal to the rectangle contained by EF, EG together with the rectangle contained by EF, GH (2.1). Therefore the rectangle contained by EF, GH, which is the remainder when FG is taken from FH, is equal to the remainder when AC is taken from AB, namely DB (CN3). Call this rectangle KH.

**Step 6.** AB is medial, so it is equal to the square on a medial straight line (Step 1); and FH, equal to AB, is that square applied to the rational straight line EF with breadth EH. Therefore EH is rational and incommensurable in length with EF (10.22). In the same way, since AC is medial and FG, equal to AC, is applied to EF with breadth EG, EG is rational and incommensurable in length with EF (10.22).

**Step 7.** DB is rational, and KH, equal to DB, is a rational area applied to the rational straight line EF, producing GH as breadth. Therefore GH is rational and commensurable in length with EF (10.20).

**Step 8.** GH is commensurable in length with EF (Step 7), and EF is incommensurable in length with EG (Step 6). Hence GH is incommensurable in length with EG (10.13).

**Step 9.** EG and GH are each rational (Steps 6, 7); therefore the square on EG and the square on GH are each commensurable with the square on EF, that is, each is a rational area (D10.1.3, D10.1.4). Being both commensurable with the square on EF, the squares on EG, GH are commensurable with one another (10.12).

**Step 10.** The square on EG and the rectangle contained by EG, GH are parallelograms under the same height EG, standing on the bases EG and GH respectively; therefore, as EG is to GH, so is the square on EG to the rectangle EG, GH (6.1). Since EG is incommensurable in length with GH (Step 8), the square on EG is incommensurable with the rectangle EG, GH (10.11).

**Step 11.** Since the squares on EG, GH are commensurable with one another (Step 9), their sum, the squares on EG, GH together, is commensurable with the square on EG (10.15). But the square on EG is incommensurable with the rectangle EG, GH (Step 10); therefore the sum of the squares on EG, GH is incommensurable with the rectangle EG, GH (10.13).

**Step 12.** Twice the rectangle EG, GH has to the rectangle EG, GH the ratio 2 : 1, which a number has to a number; therefore twice the rectangle EG, GH is commensurable with the rectangle EG, GH (10.6). But the rectangle EG, GH is incommensurable with the sum of the squares on EG, GH (Step 11); therefore twice the rectangle EG, GH is incommensurable with the sum of the squares on EG, GH (10.13).

**Step 13.** Since the straight line EH is cut at G, the square on EH is equal to the squares on EG, GH together with twice the rectangle contained by EG, GH (2.4). Thus the square on EH is the sum of two incommensurable magnitudes, namely the sum of the squares on EG, GH and twice the rectangle EG, GH (Step 12); therefore the square on EH is incommensurable with each of them, and in particular with the sum of the squares on EG, GH (10.16).

**Step 14.** The sum of the squares on EG, GH is commensurable with the square on EG (Step 11), and the square on EG is commensurable with the square on EF (Step 9); therefore the sum of the squares on EG, GH is commensurable with the square on EF (10.12), that is, it is a rational area (D10.1.4).

**Step 15.** The square on EH is incommensurable with the sum of the squares on EG, GH (Step 13), and that sum is commensurable with the square on EF (Step 14); therefore the square on EH is incommensurable with the square on EF (10.13). Hence the square on EH is irrational, and EH, the straight line which produces it, is irrational (D10.1.4, D10.1.3).

**Step 16.** But EH is rational (Step 6). Thus EH is both rational and irrational, which is impossible. Therefore the supposition of Step 2 is false, and a medial area does not exceed a medial area by a rational area. Q.E.D.

result.statement: To find medial straight lines commensurable in square only which contain a rational rectangle.
result.proof:
**Step 1.** Let A be the assigned rational straight line. By 10.10 find a straight line B incommensurable in length only with A, that is, such that the square on B is commensurable with the square on A while B is incommensurable in length with A. Then B is commensurable in square with A (D10.1.2), and since A is rational, B is rational also (D10.1.3). Thus A, B are two rational straight lines commensurable in square only.

**Step 2.** Between A and B take a mean proportional C (6.13), so that A : C = C : B.

**Step 3.** To the three straight lines A, B, C find a fourth proportional D (6.12), so that A : B = C : D.

**Step 4.** Since A : C = C : B, the three straight lines A, C, B are proportional; therefore the rectangle contained by the extremes A, B is equal to the square on the mean C (6.17).

**Step 5.** Since A, B are rational straight lines commensurable in square only, the rectangle A, B is irrational, and the side of the square equal to it is medial (10.21). But the square on C is equal to the rectangle A, B (Step 4); therefore C is medial (10.21).

**Step 6.** Since A : B = C : D, and A is incommensurable in length with B (Step 1), therefore C is incommensurable in length with D (10.11).

**Step 7.** Again, since the four straight lines A, B, C, D are proportional, the squares on them, being similar figures similarly described upon them, are also proportional: sq(A) : sq(B) = sq(C) : sq(D) (6.22). But the square on A is commensurable with the square on B, since A, B are commensurable in square (D10.1.2); therefore the square on C is commensurable with the square on D (10.11), that is, C and D are commensurable in square (D10.1.2).

**Step 8.** From Steps 6 and 7, C, D are commensurable in square only. And C is medial (Step 5), and D is commensurable with C (in square); therefore D is also medial (10.23). Therefore C, D are medial straight lines commensurable in square only.

**Step 9.** Since A : B = C : D, alternately A : C = B : D (5.16).

**Step 10.** But A : C = C : B (Step 2). Since the ratios C : B and B : D are each the same as the ratio A : C, therefore C : B = B : D (5.11).

**Step 11.** Hence C, B, D are three proportional straight lines, so the rectangle contained by the extremes C, D is equal to the square on the mean B (6.17).

**Step 12.** Now the square on A, the assigned rational straight line, is rational (D10.1.4), and the square on B is commensurable with it (Step 1); therefore the square on B is rational (D10.1.4). The rectangle C, D, being equal to the square on B (Step 11), is measured by the same measure as the square on B and is therefore commensurable with the square on A (D10.1.1); hence the rectangle C, D is rational (D10.1.4).

**Step 13.** Therefore C, D are medial straight lines commensurable in square only (Step 8) which contain a rational rectangle (Step 12); that is, medial straight lines commensurable in square only which contain a rational rectangle have been found. Q.E.F.

result.statement: To find medial straight lines commensurable in square only which contain a medial rectangle.
result.proof:
## Proposition 10.28
**Statement:** To find medial straight lines commensurable in square only which contain a medial rectangle.

**Step 1.** Let three rational straight lines A, B, C be set out which are commensurable in square only, each with each: that is, any two of them have squares that are commensurable, while the lines themselves are incommensurable in length [D10.1.2].

**Step 2.** Let D be taken a mean proportional between A and B [6.13], so that A : D = D : B; and let E be taken a fourth proportional to the three straight lines B, C, D [6.12], so that B : C = D : E.

**Step 3.** Since A : D = D : B, the three straight lines A, D, B are proportional; therefore the rectangle contained by the extremes A, B is equal to the square on the mean D [6.17].

**Step 4.** Since A, B are rational straight lines commensurable in square only, the rectangle A, B is medial, and the side of the square equal to it is a medial straight line [10.21]. But the square on D is equal to the rectangle A, B (Step 3); therefore D, the side of that square, is medial.

**Step 5.** Since B : C = D : E, and the first, B, is incommensurable in length with the second, C (Step 1), the third, D, is also incommensurable in length with the fourth, E [10.11].

**Step 6.** Again, since the four straight lines B, C, D, E are proportional, the squares on them, being similar figures similarly described on proportional straight lines, are also proportional: sq(B) : sq(C) = sq(D) : sq(E) [6.22]. And sq(B) is commensurable with sq(C) (Step 1); therefore sq(D) is commensurable with sq(E) [10.11].

**Step 7.** By Steps 5 and 6, D and E are commensurable in square [D10.1.2] but incommensurable in length; that is, D, E are commensurable in square only.

**Step 8.** D is medial (Step 4), and E is commensurable with D, namely in square (Step 6); but a straight line commensurable with a medial straight line is medial [10.23]. Therefore E is also medial.

**Step 9.** Therefore D, E are medial straight lines commensurable in square only. It remains to show that the rectangle contained by D, E is medial.

**Step 10.** Since B : C = D : E (Step 2), alternately B : D = C : E [5.16].

**Step 11.** Since A : D = D : B (Step 2), inversely B : D = D : A [5.7].

**Step 12.** The ratios D : A (Step 11) and C : E (Step 10) are each the same as the ratio B : D; therefore D : A = C : E [5.11].

**Step 13.** Since the four straight lines D, A, C, E are proportional, the rectangle contained by the extremes D, E is equal to the rectangle contained by the means A, C [6.16].

**Step 14.** But A, C are rational straight lines commensurable in square only (Step 1); therefore the rectangle A, C is medial, that is, it is equal to the square on a medial straight line [10.21]. The rectangle D, E is equal to the rectangle A, C (Step 13), and therefore equal to that same square [CN1]; hence the rectangle D, E is also medial.

**Step 15.** Therefore medial straight lines D, E, commensurable in square only, have been found which contain a medial rectangle, namely the rectangle D, E. Q.E.F.

Note on path: the three rational straight lines commensurable in square only are taken as data set out at the start (as in 10.27, where two such lines are set out); no separate construction of them is invoked, so the proof cites no result for their existence.

result.statement: To find two rational straight lines commensurable in square only and such that the square on the greater is greater than the square on the less by the square on a straight line commensurable in length with the greater.
result.proof:
**Step 1.** Let AB be the assigned rational straight line [D10.1.3]. We shall find a second rational straight line, commensurable in square only with AB, greater than AB, and whose square exceeds the square on AB by the square on a straight line commensurable in length with that greater line.

**Step 2.** Let two square numbers CD, DE be set out, CD the greater, with the points C, E, D placed in order so that CD = CE + ED, and such that the difference CE is not a square number. Such numbers exist: for example the square numbers 3·3 = 9 and 2·2 = 4 [D7.18] have difference 5, and 5 is not a square number, since 2·2 = 4 < 5 < 9 = 3·3 while no number lies between 2 and 3, so no number multiplied by itself gives 5 [D7.18].

**Step 3.** The number CD has not to the number CE the ratio which a square number has to a square number. For if CD had to CE such a ratio, then, since the first, CD, is square, the second, CE, would also be square [8.24]; but CE is not square (Step 2).

**Step 4.** From the point B let BF be drawn at right angles to AB [1.11], and let its length be so taken that, as the number CE is to the number DE, so is the square on AB to the square on BF [10.6, Porism: given the straight line AB and the numbers CE, DE, a straight line can be found such that the square on AB has to the square on it the ratio CE : DE]. Join AF [P1].

**Step 5.** Since the angle ABF is right, the square on AF is equal to the squares on AB, BF together [1.47].

**Step 6.** Since, as the square on AB is to the square on BF, so is CE to ED (Step 4), therefore componendo, as the square on AB together with the square on BF is to the square on BF, so is CE together with ED to ED [5.18]; that is, by Step 5 and Step 2, as the square on AF is to the square on BF, so is the number CD to the number DE.

**Step 7.** Again, since as the square on AF is to the square on BF, so is CD to DE (Step 6), therefore convertendo, as the square on AF is to the excess of the square on AF over the square on BF, so is CD to the excess of CD over DE [5.19, Porism]. But the excess of the square on AF over the square on BF is the square on AB (Step 5), and the excess of CD over DE is CE (Step 2). Therefore, as the square on AF is to the square on AB, so is the number CD to the number CE.

**Step 8.** Thus the square on AF has to the square on AB the ratio which a number, CD, has to a number, CE; therefore the square on AF is commensurable with the square on AB [10.6]. Hence AF is commensurable in square with AB [D10.1.2]; and AB is rational, so AF is rational [D10.1.3].

**Step 9.** But CD has not to CE the ratio which a square number has to a square number (Step 3); therefore neither has the square on AF to the square on AB that ratio (Step 7); therefore AF is incommensurable in length with AB [10.9]. Consequently AF, AB are rational straight lines commensurable in square only.

**Step 10.** The square on AF is equal to the squares on AB, BF together (Step 5); hence the square on AF is greater than the square on AB, its part [CN5], so that AF is the greater of the two straight lines, and the square on the greater, AF, is greater than the square on the less, AB, by the square on BF.

**Step 11.** Now, as the square on AF is to the square on BF, so is CD to DE (Step 6), and CD, DE are square numbers; therefore the square on AF has to the square on BF the ratio which a square number has to a square number, so that AF is commensurable in length with BF [10.9].

**Step 12.** Therefore two rational straight lines AF, AB have been found which are commensurable in square only (Steps 8, 9), and such that the square on the greater, AF, is greater than the square on the less, AB, by the square on BF (Step 10), a straight line commensurable in length with the greater, AF (Step 11). Q.E.F.

Path note: the right-angled triangle is obtained by erecting the perpendicular BF at B and taking AF as hypotenuse, rather than by fitting a chord into a semicircle on AB; this avoids having to show that the chord found from the number ratio is shorter than the diameter, and it lets the given rational line serve as the lesser of the two lines found.

result.statement: To find two rational straight lines commensurable in square only and such that the square on the greater is greater is greater than the square on the less by the square on a straight line incommensurable in length with the greater.
result.proof:
**Step 1.** Let AB be the assigned rational straight line [D10.1.3]. Let there be taken two square numbers CE, ED, so that CD is their sum, and such that CD is not a square number. Such numbers exist: for instance CE = 4 (= 2·2) and ED = 9 (= 3·3) are square numbers [D7.18], and their sum CD = 13 is not square, since it exceeds 9 = 3·3 and falls short of 16 = 4·4, while no number lies between 3 and 4. Since CE is a part of CD, DC is greater than CE, and the excess of CD over CE is ED.

**Step 2.** Let AB be bisected at O [1.10], and with centre O and distance OA let the circle AFB be described [P3]. Then AB, passing through the centre O and terminated at both ends by the circumference, is a diameter of this circle, and the figure contained by AB and the circumference on one side of it is the semicircle AFB on AB [D1.18].

**Step 3.** Using the numbers DC, CE and the straight line BA, let a straight line H be found, by the porism to 10.6, such that, as DC is to CE, so is the square on BA to the square on H [10.6].

**Step 4.** Since DC is greater than CE, and, as DC is to CE, so is the square on BA to the square on H, the square on BA is greater than the square on H [5.14]; hence BA is greater than H, for the square on the greater straight line is the greater. Thus H is not greater than the diameter AB of the circle AFB.

**Step 5.** Let there be fitted into the circle AFB, from the point A on the diameter AB, the straight line AF equal to H [4.1], and let FB be joined [P1]. Since AF is less than the diameter AB, the point F lies on the circumference and is distinct from A and B; therefore the angle AFB is an angle in the semicircle on AB, and so the angle AFB is right [3.31].

**Step 6.** Therefore the square on AB is equal to the squares on AF, FB [1.47]; so that the square on AB exceeds the square on AF by the square on BF, and AB is the greater of AB, AF.

**Step 7.** Since AF is equal to H, the square on AF is equal to the square on H; therefore, as DC is to CE, so is the square on BA to the square on AF. Thus the square on BA has to the square on AF the ratio which the number DC has to the number CE; therefore the square on BA is commensurable with the square on AF [10.6].

**Step 8.** Therefore BA, AF are commensurable in square [D10.1.2]. And BA is the assigned rational straight line; therefore AF, being commensurable in square with BA, is also rational [D10.1.3].

**Step 9.** Now DC has not to CE the ratio which a square number has to a square number. For, if it had, then inversely CE would have to DC the ratio which a square number has to a square number [5.7]; and CE is a square number; therefore DC would also be a square number [8.24]: but by construction CD is not square. Therefore DC has not to CE the ratio which a square number has to a square number.

**Step 10.** Hence neither has the square on BA to the square on AF the ratio which a square number has to a square number; therefore BA is incommensurable in length with AF [10.9]. Therefore BA, AF are rational straight lines commensurable in square only.

**Step 11.** Again, since, as DC is to CE, so is the square on AB to the square on AF, therefore, convertendo, as CD is to the excess of CD over CE, so is the square on AB to the excess of the square on AB over the square on AF [5.19]. But the excess of CD over CE is DE, and, by Step 6, the excess of the square on AB over the square on AF is the square on BF. Therefore, as CD is to DE, so is the square on AB to the square on BF.

**Step 12.** But CD has not to DE the ratio which a square number has to a square number. For, if it had, then inversely DE would have to CD the ratio which a square number has to a square number [5.7]; and DE is a square number; therefore CD would also be a square number [8.24]: which it is not. Therefore CD has not to DE the ratio which a square number has to a square number.

**Step 13.** Hence neither has the square on AB to the square on BF the ratio which a square number has to a square number; therefore AB is incommensurable in length with BF [10.9].

**Step 14.** And, by Step 6, the square on AB is equal to the squares on AF, FB; therefore the square on AB is greater than the square on AF by the square on BF, and BF is incommensurable in length with AB.

**Step 15.** Therefore two rational straight lines AB, AF have been found which are commensurable in square only, and such that the square on the greater, AB, is greater than the square on the less, AF, by the square on a straight line, BF, incommensurable in length with the greater, AB. Q.E.F.

result.statement: To find two medial straight lines commensurable in square only, containing a rational rectangle, and such that the square on the greater is greater than the square on the less by the square on a straight line commensurable in length with the greater.
result.proof:
**Step 1.** Let two rational straight lines A, B, commensurable in square only, be set out such that A is the greater and the square on A is greater than the square on B by the square on a straight line commensurable in length with A [10.29].

**Step 2.** Let the square on C be equal to the rectangle A, B [2.14]. Since A, B are rational straight lines commensurable in square only, the rectangle A, B is irrational and the side of the square equal to it is irrational and is called medial [10.21]. Therefore C is medial.

**Step 3.** To the straight line C let there be applied, in a right angle, a parallelogram equal to the square on B [1.44] (the square on B being divided by its diameter into two triangles, which are applied to C in succession); being right-angled, it is a rectangle contained by C and its other side. Let that other side be D, so that the rectangle C, D is equal to the square on B.

**Step 4.** B is rational; therefore the square on B is rational [D10.1.3, D10.1.4]. And the rectangle C, D is equal to the square on B; therefore the rectangle C, D is rational [D10.1.4].

**Step 5.** The rectangle A, B and the square on B, that is, the rectangle B, B, are parallelograms of the same height B; therefore as the rectangle A, B is to the square on B, so is A to B [6.1].

**Step 6.** The rectangle A, B is equal to the square on C, and the square on B is equal to the rectangle C, D; equal magnitudes have the same ratio to the same, and the same has the same ratio to equal magnitudes [5.7]; therefore as the square on C is to the rectangle C, D, so is A to B [5.11].

**Step 7.** The square on C and the rectangle C, D are parallelograms of the same height C; therefore as the square on C is to the rectangle C, D, so is C to D [6.1]. Therefore as A is to B, so is C to D [5.11].

**Step 8.** Since A is greater than B and as A is to B, so is C to D, C is greater than D [5.14].

**Step 9.** Since A, B are commensurable in square only, A is incommensurable in length with B. And as A is to B, so is C to D; therefore C is incommensurable in length with D [10.11].

**Step 10.** Since A, B, C, D are four proportional straight lines, and the squares on them are similar figures similarly described upon them, as the square on A is to the square on B, so is the square on C to the square on D [6.22]. But the square on A is commensurable with the square on B, since A, B are commensurable in square; therefore the square on C is commensurable with the square on D [10.11]; that is, C, D are commensurable in square [D10.1.2]. With Step 9, C, D are therefore commensurable in square only.

**Step 11.** C is medial (Step 2), and D is commensurable in square with C (Step 10); but a straight line commensurable with a medial straight line is medial [10.23]. Therefore D is medial.

**Step 12.** Since A, B, C, D are proportional, and the square on A, the greater, is greater than the square on B by the square on a straight line commensurable in length with A (Step 1), the square on C, the greater (Step 8), is greater than the square on D by the square on a straight line commensurable in length with C [10.14].

**Step 13.** Therefore C, D are two medial straight lines commensurable in square only (Steps 10, 11), containing the rational rectangle C, D (Step 4), and such that the square on the greater, C, is greater than the square on the less, D, by the square on a straight line commensurable in length with C (Step 12); which was to be found.

result.statement: To find two medial straight lines commensurable in square only, containing a medial rectangle, and such that the square on the greater is greater than the square on the less by the square on a straight line commensurable with the greater.
result.proof:
**Step 1.** Let a rational straight line be set out. By 10.29 let A, C be two rational straight lines commensurable in square only, A being the greater, such that the square on A is greater than the square on C by the square on a straight line commensurable in length with A.

**Step 2.** Let B be a rational straight line commensurable in square only with each of A and C: a rational straight line commensurable in square only with an assigned rational straight line is found by 10.10, and B is taken so as to be incommensurable in length with C as well as with A. Thus A, B, C are three rational straight lines commensurable in square only.

**Step 3.** Between A and B take a mean proportional D [6.13], so that A : D = D : B. Since the three straight lines A, D, B are proportional, the rectangle contained by the extremes is equal to the square on the mean [6.17]; therefore sq(D) = rect(A, B).

**Step 4.** A and B are rational straight lines commensurable in square only; therefore rect(A, B) is irrational, and the side of the square equal to it is medial [10.21]. Since sq(D) = rect(A, B), D is medial.

**Step 5.** To the three straight lines D, B, C find a fourth proportional E [6.12], so that D : B = C : E. Since the four straight lines D, B, C, E are proportional, the rectangle contained by the extremes is equal to the rectangle contained by the means [6.16]; therefore rect(D, E) = rect(B, C).

**Step 6.** By Step 3, A : D = D : B, and by Step 5, D : B = C : E; therefore A : D = C : E [5.11]. Alternately, A : C = D : E [5.16].

**Step 7.** A is incommensurable in length with C (Step 1). Since A : C = D : E, D is also incommensurable in length with E [10.11].

**Step 8.** Since A : C = D : E, the squares on A, C and on D, E, being similar figures similarly described on proportional straight lines, are proportional: sq(A) : sq(C) = sq(D) : sq(E) [6.22]. Now sq(A) is commensurable with sq(C), because A, C are commensurable in square (Step 1); therefore sq(D) is commensurable with sq(E) [10.11]. Together with Step 7, D and E are commensurable in square only.

**Step 9.** D is medial (Step 4), and E is commensurable in square with D (Step 8); therefore E is also medial [10.23].

**Step 10.** Since A : C = D : E, and the square on A is greater than the square on C by the square on a straight line commensurable with A (Step 1), the square on D is greater than the square on E by the square on a straight line commensurable with D [10.14]. In particular D is the greater of D, E.

**Step 11.** By Step 5, rect(D, E) = rect(B, C). B and C are rational straight lines commensurable in square only (Step 2); therefore rect(B, C) is a medial area, the side of the square equal to it being medial [10.21]. Hence rect(D, E), being equal to rect(B, C), is medial.

**Step 12.** Therefore D, E are two medial straight lines commensurable in square only, containing the medial rectangle rect(D, E), and such that the square on the greater, D, is greater than the square on the less, E, by the square on a straight line commensurable with the greater. Q.E.F.

result.statement: To find two straight lines incommensurable in square which make the sum of the squares on them rational but the rectangle contained by them medial.
result.proof:
## Proposition 10.33
**Statement:** To find two straight lines incommensurable in square which make the sum of the squares on them rational but the rectangle contained by them medial.

**Step 1.** Set out two rational straight lines AB, BC commensurable in square only, AB being the greater, such that the square on AB is greater than the square on BC by the square on a straight line incommensurable in length with AB [10.30].

**Step 2.** Bisect BC at D [1.10]. Then BC is double of BD, so that the square on BD is the fourth part of the square on BC.

**Step 3.** Since BC is less than AB, BD is less than the half of AB, so the square on BD is not greater than the square on the half of AB. Apply to AB a parallelogram equal to the square on BD and deficient by a square figure [6.28]; let it be the rectangle contained by AE, EB, the point E lying on AB.

**Step 4.** AB, BC are unequal straight lines, the square on AB is greater than the square on BC by the square on a straight line incommensurable with AB, and to AB there has been applied a parallelogram equal to the fourth part of the square on BC (namely the square on BD) and deficient by a square figure, dividing AB at E. Therefore AE, EB are incommensurable in length [10.18].

**Step 5.** Bisect AB at G [1.10]; with centre G and distance GA describe a circle [P3], and let AFB be the semicircle on AB. From E draw EF at right angles to AB [1.11], meeting the semicircle at F, and join AF, FB [P1].

**Step 6.** Since AB is a diameter and F lies on the circumference, the angle AFB in the semicircle is right [3.31].

**Step 7.** In the right-angled triangle AFB the straight line FE has been drawn from the right angle at F perpendicular to the base AB; therefore the triangles AEF, FEB adjoining the perpendicular are similar both to the whole triangle AFB and to one another [6.8].

**Step 8.** Since triangle AFB is similar to triangle AEF (the angle at A common, the right angles at F and E equal), the sides subtending the equal angles are proportional [6.4]: as AB is to AF, so is AF to AE. Therefore the rectangle AB, AE is equal to the square on AF [6.17].

**Step 9.** Likewise, since triangle AFB is similar to triangle FEB (the angle at B common), as AB is to BF, so is BF to BE [6.4]; therefore the rectangle AB, BE is equal to the square on BF [6.17].

**Step 10.** Since triangle AEF is similar to triangle FEB, as AE is to EF, so is EF to EB [6.4]; therefore the rectangle AE, EB is equal to the square on EF [6.17].

**Step 11.** Again, from the similarity of triangles AFB, FEB, the side AB subtending the right angle at F is to the side FB subtending the right angle at E as the side AF subtending the angle at B is to the side FE subtending the same angle at B [6.4]: as AB is to FB, so is AF to FE. Therefore the rectangle contained by the extremes AB, FE is equal to the rectangle contained by the means FB, AF [6.16]; that is, the rectangle AB, EF is equal to the rectangle AF, FB.

**Step 12.** The rectangles AB, AE and AB, EB are parallelograms under the same height AB on the bases AE, EB; therefore as AE is to EB, so is the rectangle AB, AE to the rectangle AB, EB [6.1]. But AE is incommensurable with EB (Step 4); therefore the rectangle AB, AE is incommensurable with the rectangle AB, EB [10.11]. By Steps 8 and 9 these rectangles are the squares on AF, FB; hence the square on AF is incommensurable with the square on FB, so that AF, FB are incommensurable in square [D10.1.2].

**Step 13.** Since the angle AFB is right, the squares on AF, FB are together equal to the square on AB [1.47]. And AB is rational, so the square on AB is rational [D10.1.4]; therefore the sum of the squares on AF, FB is rational.

**Step 14.** The rectangle AE, EB is equal to the square on EF (Step 10), and by construction the rectangle AE, EB is equal to the square on BD (Step 3); therefore the square on EF is equal to the square on BD [CN1], so that EF is equal to BD, and BC is double of EF.

**Step 15.** The rectangles AB, BC and AB, EF are under the same height AB on the bases BC, EF; therefore as BC is to EF, so is the rectangle AB, BC to the rectangle AB, EF [6.1]. But BC is double of EF, so BC has to EF the ratio which the number 2 has to the number 1; therefore the rectangle AB, BC has to the rectangle AB, EF the ratio which a number has to a number, and so the rectangle AB, BC is commensurable with the rectangle AB, EF [10.6].

**Step 16.** Since AB, BC are rational straight lines commensurable in square only, the rectangle AB, BC is medial [10.21]. And an area commensurable with a medial area is medial [10.23]; therefore the rectangle AB, EF is medial.

**Step 17.** But the rectangle AB, EF is equal to the rectangle AF, FB (Step 11); therefore the rectangle AF, FB is medial.

**Step 18.** Therefore two straight lines AF, FB have been found which are incommensurable in square (Step 12), which make the sum of the squares on them rational (Step 13), but the rectangle contained by them medial (Step 17). Q.E.F.

**USED:** 10.30, 1.10, 6.28, 10.18, P3, 1.11, P1, 3.31, 6.8, 6.4, 6.17, 6.16, 6.1, 10.11, D10.1.2, 1.47, D10.1.4, CN1, 10.6, 10.21, 10.23

result.statement: To find two straight lines incommensurable in square which make the sum of the squares on them medial but the rectangle contained by them rational.
result.proof:
**Statement:** To find two straight lines incommensurable in square which make the sum of the squares on them medial but the rectangle contained by them rational.

Notation: sq(X) denotes the square on X; rect(X, Y) the rectangle contained by X and Y.

**Step 1.** By 10.31, taken in the form noted at its close (its construction carried out from the two rational straight lines commensurable in square only furnished by 10.30 in place of those of 10.29), set out two medial straight lines AB, BC commensurable in square only, containing a rational rectangle rect(AB, BC), AB being the greater, and such that sq(AB) is greater than sq(BC) by the square on a straight line incommensurable in length with AB.

**Step 2.** Bisect AB at G and BC at E (1.10). With centre G and distance GA describe a circle (P3), and let ADB be the semicircle on AB lying on one side of it. Since BC is less than AB, its half BE is less than GB, the half of AB, so sq(BE) is not greater than sq(GB), the square described on the half of AB; hence by 6.28 a parallelogram equal to sq(BE) and deficient by a square figure can be applied to AB. Let it be rect(AF, FB), F lying on AB, so that rect(AF, FB) = sq(BE).

**Step 3.** Since BC is double BE, sq(BC) is four times sq(BE); thus rect(AF, FB), which equals sq(BE), is the fourth part of sq(BC), and it has been applied to the greater line AB deficient by a square figure. Since sq(AB) exceeds sq(BC) by the square on a straight line incommensurable with AB (Step 1), 10.18 shows that AF is incommensurable in length with FB.

**Step 4.** From the point F draw FD at right angles to AB (1.11), meeting the semicircle at D, and join AD, DB (P1). Since ADB is an angle in a semicircle, the angle ADB is right (3.31). Thus in the right-angled triangle ADB the perpendicular DF has been drawn from the right angle to the base AB; therefore the triangles ADF, DBF are each similar to the whole triangle ADB and to one another (6.8).

**Step 5.** Since triangle ABD is equiangular with triangle ADF, BA : AD = AD : AF (6.4); therefore sq(AD) = rect(BA, AF) (6.17). Since triangle ABD is equiangular with triangle DBF, AB : BD = BD : BF (6.4); therefore sq(DB) = rect(AB, BF) (6.17). Since triangle ADF is equiangular with triangle DBF, AF : DF = DF : FB (6.4); therefore sq(DF) = rect(AF, FB) (6.17).

**Step 6.** The rectangles rect(BA, AF) and rect(AB, BF) have the same height AB, so rect(BA, AF) : rect(AB, BF) = AF : FB (6.1). Since AF is incommensurable in length with FB (Step 3), rect(BA, AF) is incommensurable with rect(AB, BF) (10.11). By Step 5 these rectangles are equal to sq(AD) and sq(DB) respectively; therefore sq(AD) is incommensurable with sq(DB), that is, AD and DB are incommensurable in square (D10.1.2).

**Step 7.** Since the angle ADB is right, sq(AD) + sq(DB) = sq(AB) (1.47). But AB is a medial straight line, so the square on it is a medial area (10.21). Therefore the sum of the squares on AD, DB is medial.

**Step 8.** By Step 5, sq(DF) = rect(AF, FB), and by Step 2, rect(AF, FB) = sq(BE); therefore sq(DF) = sq(BE) (CN1), and consequently DF = BE. Since BC is double BE, BC is double DF.

**Step 9.** The rectangles rect(AB, BC) and rect(AB, DF) have the same height AB, so rect(AB, BC) : rect(AB, DF) = BC : DF (6.1), which is the ratio 2 : 1, the ratio which a number has to a number; therefore rect(AB, BC) is commensurable with rect(AB, DF) (10.6). But rect(AB, BC) is rational (Step 1), that is, commensurable with the square on the assigned rational straight line (D10.1.4); hence rect(AB, DF), being commensurable with rect(AB, BC), is commensurable with that same square (10.12), and is therefore rational (D10.1.4).

**Step 10.** The rectangle contained by AD, DB is a parallelogram having the same base DB as the triangle ADB and lying in the same parallels, because its side AD is at right angles to DB; hence rect(AD, DB) is double the triangle ADB (1.41). Again, the rectangle contained by AB, DF is a parallelogram on the base AB lying in the same parallels as the triangle ADB, because DF is the perpendicular from D to AB; hence rect(AB, DF) is also double the triangle ADB (1.41). Therefore rect(AD, DB) = rect(AB, DF) (CN1), and by Step 9 rect(AD, DB) is rational.

**Step 11.** Therefore AD, DB are two straight lines incommensurable in square (Step 6) which make the sum of the squares on them medial (Step 7) but the rectangle contained by them rational (Step 10). Q.E.F.

Path note: the equality rect(AD, DB) = rect(AB, DF) in Step 10 could equally be obtained from the similar triangles ABD, DBF of Step 4 (AB : BD = AD : DF, whence the rectangles are equal by 6.16); the area route through 1.41 was chosen as the more direct.

result.statement: To find two straight lines incommensurable in square which make the sum of the squares on them medial and the rectangle contained by them medial and moreover incommensurable with the sum of the squares on them.
result.proof:
**Step 1.** Let there be set out two medial straight lines AB, BC commensurable in square only, containing a medial rectangle, and such that the square on the greater, AB, is greater than the square on the less, BC, by the square on a straight line incommensurable in length with AB [10.32; the remark with which that proposition closes furnishes precisely this variant, in which the excess is the square on a straight line incommensurable with the greater]. Since AB, BC are commensurable in square only, AB is incommensurable in length with BC [D10.1.2]; and since the square on AB exceeds the square on BC, AB is greater than BC.

**Step 2.** Let BC be bisected at F [1.10]. Then BC is double of BF, so the square on BC is four times the square on BF; that is, the square on BF is the fourth part of the square on BC. Since BC is less than AB, BF is less than the half of AB, so the square on BF does not exceed the square described on the half of AB. Therefore let there be applied to AB a parallelogram equal to the square on BF and deficient by a square figure [6.28]; let it be the rectangle contained by AE, EB, the point E lying on AB.

**Step 3.** AB, BC are two unequal straight lines, the square on the greater AB is greater than the square on the less BC by the square on a straight line incommensurable with AB, and to AB there has been applied a parallelogram equal to the fourth part of the square on BC and deficient by a square figure, dividing AB into AE, EB; therefore AE is incommensurable in length with EB [10.18].

**Step 4.** Let AB be bisected at G [1.10], and with centre G and distance GA let the semicircle ADB be described on AB [P3]; from E let ED be drawn at right angles to AB, meeting the semicircle at D [1.11]; and let AD, DB be joined [P1]. Since the angle ADB is in a semicircle, it is right [3.31].

**Step 5.** In the right-angled triangle ADB the perpendicular DE has been drawn from the right angle to the base AB; therefore the triangles ADE, DBE are similar to the whole triangle ADB and to one another [6.8]. Hence: (a) as BA is to AD, so is AD to AE, so that the square on AD is equal to the rectangle BA, AE [6.17]; (b) as AB is to BD, so is BD to BE, so that the square on BD is equal to the rectangle AB, BE [6.17]; (c) as AE is to ED, so is ED to EB, so that the square on ED is equal to the rectangle AE, EB [6.17]; (d) as AB is to BD, so is AD to DE, so that the rectangle AB, DE is equal to the rectangle AD, DB [6.16].

**Step 6.** The rectangles BA, AE and AB, BE have the same height AB; therefore, as AE is to EB, so is the rectangle BA, AE to the rectangle AB, BE [6.1]. But AE is incommensurable in length with EB (Step 3); therefore the rectangle BA, AE is incommensurable with the rectangle AB, BE [10.11], that is, the square on AD is incommensurable with the square on DB (Step 5a, 5b). Therefore AD, DB are incommensurable in square [D10.1.2].

**Step 7.** Since the angle ADB is right, the squares on AD, DB together are equal to the square on AB [1.47]. But AB is medial, so the square on AB is a medial area; therefore the sum of the squares on AD, DB is medial.

**Step 8.** The square on ED is equal to the rectangle AE, EB (Step 5c), which is equal to the square on BF (Step 2); and since squares on unequal straight lines are unequal, ED is equal to BF. Hence BC is double of ED. Now the rectangles AB, BC and AB, DE have the same height AB, so that, as BC is to DE, so is the rectangle AB, BC to the rectangle AB, DE [6.1]; therefore the rectangle AB, BC is double of the rectangle AB, DE. Thus these two rectangles have to one another the ratio which the number 2 has to the number 1, and they are commensurable [10.6].

**Step 9.** The rectangle AB, BC is medial (Step 1), and the rectangle AB, DE is commensurable with it (Step 8); therefore the rectangle AB, DE is medial [10.23, Por.]. But the rectangle AB, DE is equal to the rectangle AD, DB (Step 5d); therefore the rectangle AD, DB is medial.

**Step 10.** The square on AB and the rectangle AB, BC have the same height AB; therefore, as AB is to BC, so is the square on AB to the rectangle AB, BC [6.1]. But AB is incommensurable in length with BC (Step 1); therefore the square on AB is incommensurable with the rectangle AB, BC [10.11].

**Step 11.** The rectangle AB, BC is commensurable with the rectangle AB, DE (Step 8) and incommensurable with the square on AB (Step 10); therefore the rectangle AB, DE is incommensurable with the square on AB [10.13]. But the square on AB is equal to the sum of the squares on AD, DB (Step 7), and the rectangle AB, DE is equal to the rectangle AD, DB (Step 5d); therefore the sum of the squares on AD, DB is incommensurable with the rectangle AD, DB.

**Step 12.** Therefore two straight lines AD, DB have been found which are incommensurable in square (Step 6), which make the sum of the squares on them medial (Step 7) and the rectangle contained by them medial (Step 9), and moreover the rectangle incommensurable with the sum of the squares on them (Step 11). Q.E.F.

Note on path: the initial lines are taken from 10.32 (as its closing remark allows) rather than constructed afresh from 10.30, and the equality of the rectangles AB, DE and AD, DB is derived directly from the similar triangles of 6.8 with 6.16, this being the most direct route.

result.statement: If two rational straight lines commensurable in square only be added together, the whole is irrational; and let it be called binomial.
result.proof:
**Step 1.** Let AB, BC be two rational straight lines commensurable in square only, and let them be placed in a straight line so that AC is the whole made up of both. Let ρ denote the assigned rational straight line (D10.1.3). Since AB, BC are commensurable in square only, the squares on them have a common measure, but the lines themselves have none; that is, AB is incommensurable in length with BC (D10.1.1, D10.1.2).

**Step 2.** The rectangle contained by AB, BC and the square on BC (the rectangle contained by BC, BC) are parallelograms under the same height BC, standing on the bases AB and BC respectively. Therefore, by 6.1, as AB is to BC, so is rect(AB, BC) to sq(BC).

**Step 3.** Since AB is incommensurable in length with BC (Step 1), and AB : BC = rect(AB, BC) : sq(BC) (Step 2), it follows by 10.11 that rect(AB, BC) is incommensurable with sq(BC).

**Step 4.** Twice rect(AB, BC) has to rect(AB, BC) the ratio 2 : 1, which is the ratio of a number to a number; hence, by 10.6, 2·rect(AB, BC) is commensurable with rect(AB, BC). Now 2·rect(AB, BC) is commensurable with rect(AB, BC), and rect(AB, BC) is incommensurable with sq(BC) (Step 3); therefore, by 10.13, 2·rect(AB, BC) is incommensurable with sq(BC).

**Step 5.** Since AB, BC are commensurable in square, sq(AB) is commensurable with sq(BC) (D10.1.2). Two commensurable magnitudes being added together, by 10.15 the whole sq(AB) + sq(BC) is commensurable with each of them; in particular, sq(AB) + sq(BC) is commensurable with sq(BC), and also with sq(AB).

**Step 6.** sq(AB) + sq(BC) is commensurable with sq(BC) (Step 5), and sq(BC) is incommensurable with 2·rect(AB, BC) (Step 4); therefore, by 10.13, sq(AB) + sq(BC) is incommensurable with 2·rect(AB, BC).

**Step 7.** Since the straight line AC is cut at B, by 2.4 the square on AC is equal to the squares on AB, BC together with twice the rectangle contained by AB, BC; that is, sq(AC) = [sq(AB) + sq(BC)] + 2·rect(AB, BC). Thus sq(AC) is the whole formed by adding together the two incommensurable magnitudes sq(AB) + sq(BC) and 2·rect(AB, BC) (Step 6); hence, by 10.16, sq(AC) is incommensurable with each of them, and in particular sq(AC) is incommensurable with sq(AB) + sq(BC).

**Step 8.** The sum sq(AB) + sq(BC) is rational. For AB is rational, that is, commensurable with ρ either in length and in square or in square only (D10.1.3); in either case AB is commensurable in square with ρ, so that sq(AB) is commensurable with sq(ρ) (D10.1.2). But sq(AB) + sq(BC) is commensurable with sq(AB) (Step 5), and sq(AB) is commensurable with sq(ρ); therefore, by 10.12, sq(AB) + sq(BC) is commensurable with sq(ρ), the square on the assigned rational straight line. Hence sq(AB) + sq(BC) is a rational area (D10.1.4).

**Step 9.** sq(AC) is incommensurable with sq(AB) + sq(BC) (Step 7), and sq(AB) + sq(BC) is commensurable with sq(ρ) (Step 8); therefore, by 10.13, sq(AC) is incommensurable with sq(ρ). Consequently sq(AC) is an irrational area, and AC, the straight line on which the square equal to that area is described, is irrational (D10.1.4).

**Step 10.** Therefore, if two rational straight lines commensurable in square only be added together, the whole AC is irrational; and let it be called binomial. Q.E.D.

result.statement: If two medial straight lines commensurable in square only and containing a rational rectangle be added together, the whole is irrational; and let it be called a first bimedial straight line.
result.proof:
**Step 1.** Let AB, BC be two medial straight lines commensurable in square only and containing a rational rectangle, so that the rectangle AB·BC is rational; and let them be placed in a straight line, AC being the whole. Let ρ be the rational straight line set out. Since the rectangle AB·BC is rational, it is commensurable with the square on ρ (D10.1.4). I say that AC is irrational.

**Step 2.** Since AB, BC are commensurable in square only, the squares on AB, BC are measured by a common area and so are commensurable with one another (D10.1.2), while the straight lines AB, BC themselves have no common measure and so are incommensurable in length (D10.1.1, D10.1.2).

**Step 3.** The rectangle AB·BC and the square on BC are parallelograms under the same height BC, standing on the bases AB, BC respectively; therefore, as AB is to BC, so is the rectangle AB·BC to the square on BC (6.1).

**Step 4.** The four magnitudes AB, BC, the rectangle AB·BC, the square on BC are proportional, and the first, AB, is incommensurable with the second, BC (Step 2); therefore the third, the rectangle AB·BC, is incommensurable with the fourth, the square on BC (10.11).

**Step 5.** The square on AB is commensurable with the square on BC (Step 2); therefore, these two commensurable magnitudes being added together, the sum of the squares on AB, BC is commensurable with the square on BC (10.15).

**Step 6.** Twice the rectangle AB·BC has to the rectangle AB·BC the ratio which the number 2 has to the number 1; therefore twice the rectangle AB·BC is commensurable with the rectangle AB·BC (10.6).

**Step 7.** The sum of the squares on AB, BC is commensurable with the square on BC (Step 5), and the square on BC is incommensurable with the rectangle AB·BC (Step 4); therefore the sum of the squares on AB, BC is incommensurable with the rectangle AB·BC (10.13). Again, the rectangle AB·BC is commensurable with twice the rectangle AB·BC (Step 6), and the rectangle AB·BC is incommensurable with the sum of the squares on AB, BC; therefore twice the rectangle AB·BC is incommensurable with the sum of the squares on AB, BC (10.13).

**Step 8.** Since the straight line AC is cut at B, the square on AC is equal to the squares on AB, BC together with twice the rectangle AB·BC (2.4).

**Step 9.** The sum of the squares on AB, BC and twice the rectangle AB·BC are two incommensurable magnitudes (Step 7), and when added together they make the square on AC (Step 8); therefore the whole, the square on AC, is incommensurable with twice the rectangle AB·BC (10.16).

**Step 10.** Twice the rectangle AB·BC is commensurable with the rectangle AB·BC (Step 6), and twice the rectangle AB·BC is incommensurable with the square on AC (Step 9); therefore the rectangle AB·BC is incommensurable with the square on AC (10.13).

**Step 11.** The rectangle AB·BC is commensurable with the square on ρ (Step 1), and the rectangle AB·BC is incommensurable with the square on AC (Step 10); therefore the square on ρ is incommensurable with the square on AC (10.13).

**Step 12.** But an area incommensurable with the square on the rational straight line set out is irrational, and the straight line whose square is equal to an irrational area is irrational (D10.1.4); therefore the square on AC is irrational, and hence AC itself is irrational.

**Step 13.** Therefore, if two medial straight lines commensurable in square only and containing a rational rectangle be added together, the whole is irrational; and let it be called a first bimedial straight line.

result.statement: If two medial straight lines commensurable in square only and containing a medial rectangle be added together, the whole is irrational; and let it be called a second bimedial straight line.
result.proof:
**Step 1.** Let AB, BC be two medial straight lines commensurable in square only (D10.1.2), containing a medial rectangle AB·BC, and let them be placed in a straight line so that AC is the whole. We must show that AC is irrational.

**Step 2.** Set out a rational straight line DE (D10.1.3). By 1.44 apply to DE a rectangle DF equal to the square on AC, producing DG as breadth; and by 1.44 apply to DE a rectangle EH equal to the sum of the squares on AB and BC, producing DH as breadth, so that H lies on DG.

**Step 3.** By 2.4, the square on AC equals the squares on AB, BC together with twice the rectangle AB·BC. Subtracting the equal areas EH and (sq AB + sq BC) from the equal areas DF and sq AC, the remainder HF equals twice the rectangle AB·BC (CN3); and HF is the rectangle contained by DE and HG.

**Step 4.** Since AB is medial, the square on AB is a medial area (10.21). Since AB, BC are commensurable in square, the squares on AB and BC are commensurable (D10.1.2); therefore their sum, the area EH, is commensurable with the square on AB (10.15). An area commensurable with a medial area is medial (10.23), so EH is medial.

**Step 5.** The rectangle AB·BC is medial by hypothesis. Twice this rectangle has to the rectangle itself the ratio 2 : 1, which a number has to a number, so twice the rectangle is commensurable with the rectangle (10.6). Hence HF, being twice the rectangle AB·BC, is medial (10.23).

**Step 6.** EH is a medial area applied to the rational straight line DE; therefore its breadth DH is rational and incommensurable in length with DE (10.22). Likewise HF is a medial area applied to DE, so HG is rational and incommensurable in length with DE (10.22).

**Step 7.** Since AB, BC are commensurable in square only, AB is incommensurable in length with BC. The square on AB and the rectangle AB·BC are parallelograms under the same height AB, so by 6.1, sq AB : rect AB·BC = AB : BC. Therefore the square on AB is incommensurable with the rectangle AB·BC (10.11).

**Step 8.** EH is commensurable with the square on AB (Step 4), and the square on AB is incommensurable with the rectangle AB·BC (Step 7); therefore EH is incommensurable with the rectangle AB·BC (10.13). Again, the rectangle AB·BC is commensurable with HF, its double (Step 5); therefore EH is incommensurable with HF (10.13).

**Step 9.** EH and HF are parallelograms under the same height DE with bases DH and HG, so by 6.1, EH : HF = DH : HG. Since EH is incommensurable with HF, DH is incommensurable in length with HG (10.11).

**Step 10.** Each of DH, HG is rational and incommensurable in length with DE (Step 6), hence commensurable in square only with DE; so the square on DH and the square on HG are each commensurable with the square on DE (D10.1.2), and therefore commensurable with one another (10.12). Thus DH, HG are rational straight lines commensurable in square but not in length, that is, commensurable in square only.

**Step 11.** Therefore DG, the sum of the two rational straight lines DH, HG commensurable in square only, is a binomial straight line and is irrational (10.36).

**Step 12.** DF is the rectangle contained by the rational straight line DE and the irrational straight line DG. If DF were a rational area, then, being applied to the rational straight line DE, it would produce as breadth a straight line rational and commensurable in length with DE (10.20); but its breadth DG is irrational. Therefore DF is not rational, that is, DF is an irrational area (D10.1.4).

**Step 13.** The square on AC is equal to DF and is therefore irrational; hence AC, the side of the square equal to this irrational area, is irrational (D10.1.4). Therefore the whole AC, composed of two medial straight lines commensurable in square only and containing a medial rectangle, is irrational; and let it be called a second bimedial straight line.

result.statement: If two straight lines incommensurable in square which make the sum of the squares on them rational, but the rectangle contained by them medial, be added together, the whole straight line is irrational: and let it be called major.
result.proof:
**Step 1.** Let AB, BC be two straight lines incommensurable in square, such that the sum of the squares on AB, BC is rational but the rectangle contained by AB, BC is medial; and let them be added together, so that AC is one straight line having the point B upon it. Let R denote the square on the assigned rational straight line. I say that AC is irrational.

**Step 2.** Since the rectangle AB, BC is medial, it is equal to the square on a medial straight line, that is, to a rectangle contained by rational straight lines commensurable in square only; and such a rectangle is irrational [10.21]. Therefore the rectangle AB, BC is irrational, that is, it is incommensurable with R [D10.1.4].

**Step 3.** Twice the rectangle AB, BC has to the rectangle AB, BC the ratio which the number 2 has to the unit, that is, the ratio which a number has to a number; therefore twice the rectangle AB, BC is commensurable with the rectangle AB, BC [10.6].

**Step 4.** Since twice the rectangle AB, BC is commensurable with the rectangle AB, BC [Step 3], and the rectangle AB, BC is incommensurable with R [Step 2], twice the rectangle AB, BC is also incommensurable with R [10.13]. Therefore twice the rectangle AB, BC is irrational [D10.1.4].

**Step 5.** The sum of the squares on AB, BC is rational by hypothesis, that is, it is commensurable with R [D10.1.4]. Since the sum of the squares on AB, BC is commensurable with R, and R is incommensurable with twice the rectangle AB, BC [Step 4], the sum of the squares on AB, BC is incommensurable with twice the rectangle AB, BC [10.13].

**Step 6.** Since the straight line AC is cut at B, the square on AC is equal to the squares on AB, BC together with twice the rectangle contained by AB, BC [2.4].

**Step 7.** Therefore the square on AC is the sum of two incommensurable magnitudes, namely the sum of the squares on AB, BC and twice the rectangle AB, BC [Step 5]; hence the whole, the square on AC, is incommensurable with each of them [10.16], and in particular with the sum of the squares on AB, BC.

**Step 8.** Now the sum of the squares on AB, BC is commensurable with R [Step 5] and incommensurable with the square on AC [Step 7]; therefore the square on AC is incommensurable with R [10.13]. Hence the square on AC is irrational, and therefore AC, the side of that square, is also irrational [D10.1.4].

**Step 9.** Therefore, if two straight lines incommensurable in square which make the sum of the squares on them rational but the rectangle contained by them medial be added together, the whole straight line is irrational; and let it be called major. Q.E.D.

Note on path: the irrationality of AC needs only that twice the rectangle AB, BC is incommensurable with the rational sum of the squares; this is obtained directly from 10.6 and 10.13 without first establishing that twice the rectangle is itself medial, so the longer route through the construction of an equal square and 10.23 is not required. The hypothesis that AB, BC are incommensurable in square is not needed for the irrationality itself; it serves to distinguish the major from the binomial and the bimedials.

result.statement: If two straight lines incommensurable in square which make the sum of the squares on them medial, but the rectangle contained by them rational, be added together, the whole straight line is irrational; and let it be called the side of a rational plus a medial area.
result.proof:
**Step 1.** Let AB, BC be two straight lines incommensurable in square, placed in a straight line so that AC is the whole, and let them satisfy the hypothesis: the sum of the squares on AB, BC is medial, while the rectangle AB, BC is rational. Let R denote the rational square set out (the square on the assigned rational straight line). I say that AC is irrational.

**Step 2.** Since AC is cut at B, the square on AC is equal to the squares on AB, BC together with twice the rectangle AB, BC [2.4]. Write S for the sum of the squares on AB, BC, so that the square on AC is equal to S together with twice the rectangle AB, BC.

**Step 3.** Twice the rectangle AB, BC has to the rectangle AB, BC the ratio which the number 2 has to the number 1; therefore twice the rectangle AB, BC is commensurable with the rectangle AB, BC [10.6].

**Step 4.** The rectangle AB, BC is rational, that is, it is commensurable with the rational square R [D10.1.4]. Since twice the rectangle AB, BC is commensurable with the rectangle AB, BC (Step 3), and the rectangle AB, BC is commensurable with R, twice the rectangle AB, BC is commensurable with R [10.12]; hence twice the rectangle AB, BC is rational [D10.1.4].

**Step 5.** S, the sum of the squares on AB, BC, is medial, that is, it is equal to the square on a medial straight line, which square is equal to a rectangle contained by rational straight lines commensurable in square only; such a rectangle is irrational [10.21]. Therefore S is an irrational area, that is, S is incommensurable with the rational square R [D10.1.4].

**Step 6.** Twice the rectangle AB, BC and R are commensurable (Step 4), and R is incommensurable with S (Step 5); therefore twice the rectangle AB, BC is also incommensurable with S [10.13].

**Step 7.** Thus S and twice the rectangle AB, BC are two incommensurable magnitudes, and when they are added together the whole is the square on AC (Step 2). Therefore the square on AC is incommensurable with each of them, and in particular with twice the rectangle AB, BC [10.16].

**Step 8.** Twice the rectangle AB, BC is commensurable with R (Step 4), and it is incommensurable with the square on AC (Step 7); therefore R is also incommensurable with the square on AC [10.13]. Hence the square on AC is irrational, being incommensurable with the rational square R, and therefore AC, the straight line which produces it, is irrational [D10.1.4].

**Step 9.** Therefore, if two straight lines incommensurable in square which make the sum of the squares on them medial but the rectangle contained by them rational be added together, the whole straight line is irrational; and let it be called the side of a rational plus a medial area. Q.E.D.

result.statement: If two straight lines incommensurable in square which make the sum of the squares on them medial, and the rectangle contained by them medial and also incommensurable with the sum of the squares on them, be added together, the whole straight line is irrational; and let it be called the   side of the sum of two medial areas.
result.proof:
**Step 1.** Let AB, BC be two straight lines incommensurable in square, placed in a straight line at B, such that the sum of the squares on AB, BC is medial, the rectangle AB·BC is medial, and the rectangle AB·BC is incommensurable with the sum of the squares on AB, BC. We show that the whole AC is irrational.

**Step 2.** Set out a rational straight line DE [D10.1.3]. To DE apply, at right angles, the rectangle DF equal to the sum of the squares on AB, BC, with breadth DG [1.45]; and to GF (the side of DF opposite DE) apply, at right angles and on the same side, the rectangle GH equal to twice the rectangle AB·BC, with breadth GK [1.45]. Then DK is one straight line, and the whole DH is the rectangle contained by DE, DK.

**Step 3.** By 2.4, the square on AC equals the squares on AB, BC together with twice the rectangle AB·BC. Since DF equals the squares on AB, BC and GH equals twice the rectangle AB·BC, the whole DH = DF + GH equals the square on AC [CN2, CN1].

**Step 4.** The sum of the squares on AB, BC is medial, that is, equal to the square on a medial straight line [10.21]; DF equals it [CN1], so DF is a medial area applied to the rational straight line DE. By 10.22 its breadth DG is rational and incommensurable in length with DE.

**Step 5.** The rectangle AB·BC is medial. Twice the rectangle AB·BC has to the rectangle AB·BC the ratio 2 : 1, which a number has to a number, so twice the rectangle is commensurable with the rectangle [10.6]; and an area commensurable with a medial area is medial [10.23, Porism]. Hence GH, being equal to twice the rectangle AB·BC, is medial. GH is applied to GF, which equals DE [1.34] and is therefore rational; so by 10.22 its breadth GK is rational and incommensurable in length with DE.

**Step 6.** By hypothesis the squares on AB, BC are incommensurable with the rectangle AB·BC, and the rectangle AB·BC is commensurable with twice itself (Step 5); therefore the squares on AB, BC are incommensurable with twice the rectangle AB·BC [10.13]. Hence DF is incommensurable with GH.

**Step 7.** DF and GH are parallelograms under the same height DE (= GF), so DF : GH = DG : GK [6.1]. Since DF is incommensurable with GH, DG is incommensurable in length with GK [10.11].

**Step 8.** DG and GK are each rational and each incommensurable in length with DE (Steps 4, 5); hence each is commensurable with DE in square only [D10.1.3]. The squares on DG and GK are thus both commensurable with the square on DE, so they are commensurable with one another [10.12], i.e. DG, GK are commensurable in square [D10.1.2]. Together with Step 7, DG and GK are rational straight lines commensurable in square only.

**Step 9.** Therefore DK, the sum of DG and GK, is irrational; it is a binomial [10.36].

**Step 10.** DH is contained by the rational straight line DE and the irrational straight line DK. If DH were rational, then, being a rational area applied to the rational straight line DE, it would produce as breadth a straight line rational and commensurable in length with DE [10.20]; but its breadth DK is irrational. Therefore DH is not rational, that is, DH is irrational [D10.1.4].

**Step 11.** The side of the square equal to an irrational area is irrational [D10.1.4]. Since the square on AC equals DH (Step 3), AC is the side of the square equal to DH; therefore AC is irrational. Because the square on AC is the sum of the two medial areas DF and GH, let AC be called the side of the sum of two medial areas. Q.E.D.

Remark on path choice: the applications of areas in Step 2 use 1.45 (a parallelogram in a given angle equal to any given rectilineal figure) rather than 1.44, since the figures applied are squares and rectangles rather than triangles.

result.statement: A binomial straight line is divided into its terms at one point only.
result.proof:
**Step 1.** Let AB be a binomial straight line divided into its terms at C. By the definition of a binomial (10.36), AC and CB are rational straight lines commensurable in square only; let ρ denote the assigned rational straight line with respect to which "rational" is understood (D10.1.3). Suppose, if possible, that AB is also divided into its terms at another point D, so that AD, DB are likewise rational straight lines commensurable in square only and the division at D is different from the division at C, i.e. the terms AD, DB are not the same straight lines as the terms AC, CB. In particular AD is not equal to AC (otherwise D would coincide with C), and AD is not equal to CB (otherwise DB, the remainder of AB after AD, would be equal to AC, the remainder of AB after CB (CN3), and AD, DB would be the very terms CB, AC of the division at C taken in the other order, which is the same division).

**Step 2.** The hypotheses on C and D are the same, so we may suppose that D lies between A and C (otherwise interchange the letters C and D). Then AC is made up of AD and DC, and DB is made up of DC and CB.

**Step 3.** The rectangle rect(AC, CB) is not equal to the rectangle rect(AD, DB). For suppose rect(AC, CB) = rect(AD, DB). Then the rectangle contained by the extremes AC, CB is equal to the rectangle contained by the means AD, DB, so the four straight lines are proportional (6.16): AC : AD = DB : CB, that is, (AD + DC) : AD = (CB + DC) : CB. Separando (5.17), DC : AD = DC : CB. Magnitudes to which the same magnitude has the same ratio are equal (5.9); hence AD = CB, contrary to Step 1. Therefore rect(AC, CB) ≠ rect(AD, DB).

**Step 4.** Since AB is cut at C, sq(AB) = sq(AC) + sq(CB) + 2·rect(AC, CB) (2.4); and since AB is cut at D, sq(AB) = sq(AD) + sq(DB) + 2·rect(AD, DB) (2.4). Hence (CN1) sq(AC) + sq(CB) + 2·rect(AC, CB) = sq(AD) + sq(DB) + 2·rect(AD, DB). Write P = sq(AC) + sq(CB), Q = sq(AD) + sq(DB), M = 2·rect(AC, CB), N = 2·rect(AD, DB), so that P + M = Q + N. By Step 3, M ≠ N; let the greater of M, N exceed the less by the area K. If N = M + K, then P + M = Q + M + K, and subtracting M from both sides (CN3) gives P = Q + K; if M = N + K, the same argument gives Q = P + K. Thus P and Q are unequal, and the greater of the two sums of squares exceeds the less by the same area K by which the greater of the doubled rectangles exceeds the less.

**Step 5.** P = sq(AC) + sq(CB) is a rational area. AC is rational, i.e. commensurable with ρ either in length and in square or in square only (D10.1.3); in either case AC is commensurable in square with ρ, so sq(AC) and sq(ρ) are measured by a common area (D10.1.2), i.e. sq(AC) is commensurable with sq(ρ) (D10.1.1) and therefore rational (D10.1.4). Likewise sq(CB) is rational. Again, AC and CB are commensurable in square, so sq(AC) and sq(CB) are commensurable (D10.1.2). When two commensurable magnitudes are added, the whole is commensurable with each of them (10.15); so P is commensurable with sq(AC). Since sq(AC) is commensurable with sq(ρ), P is commensurable with sq(ρ) (10.12), i.e. P is rational (D10.1.4). In the same way Q = sq(AD) + sq(DB) is rational.

**Step 6.** K is a rational area. P and Q are each commensurable with sq(ρ), hence commensurable with one another (10.12). By Step 4 the greater of P, Q is the whole made up of the less together with K. Since the whole is commensurable with one of its parts (the lesser sum), the two parts are commensurable with one another (10.15); so K is commensurable with the lesser sum, which is commensurable with sq(ρ). Hence K is commensurable with sq(ρ) (10.12), i.e. K is rational (D10.1.4).

**Step 7.** M and N are medial areas. rect(AC, CB) is contained by rational straight lines commensurable in square only, so it is a medial area, being equal to the square on a medial straight line (10.21). Its double M = rect(AC, CB) + rect(AC, CB) is measured by rect(AC, CB), so M is commensurable with rect(AC, CB) (D10.1.1); and an area commensurable with a medial area is medial (10.23, Porism). Therefore M is medial. In the same way, since AD, DB are rational straight lines commensurable in square only, rect(AD, DB) is medial (10.21) and its double N is medial (D10.1.1, 10.23).

**Step 8.** By Step 4 the greater of the areas M, N exceeds the less by K; by Step 7 both M and N are medial; and by Step 6 K is rational.
