Thus a medial area exceeds a medial area by a rational area, which is impossible (10.26). This contradiction shows that no point D other than C divides AB into rational straight lines commensurable in square only forming a different pair of terms. Therefore a binomial straight line is divided into its terms at one point only. Q.E.D.

result.statement: A first bimedial straight line is divided at one point only.
result.proof:
**Step 1.** Let AB be a first bimedial straight line divided into its terms at C. By the definition of a first bimedial (10.37), AC and CB are medial straight lines, commensurable in square only, and the rectangle contained by AC, CB is rational. Suppose, if possible, that AB is also divided at another point D into terms of the same kind, so that AD, DB are medial straight lines commensurable in square only containing a rational rectangle, the division at D being a different division of AB into its terms from that at C. We derive a contradiction.

**Step 2.** AD is not equal to CB. For if AD were equal to CB, then, subtracting these equals from the whole AB, the remainder DB would equal the remainder AC (CN3); the terms AD, DB would then be the very straight lines CB, AC, so that the division at D would consist of exactly the same two terms as the division at C, only named in the other order, which is not a different division of AB into its terms, contrary to the supposition of Step 1.

**Step 3.** Bisect AB at E (1.10), so that AE = EB. Neither C nor D coincides with E. For if C coincided with E, then AC = CB, and two equal straight lines are measured by the same measure (each of them measures both), so AC, CB would be commensurable in length (D10.1.1), whereas they are commensurable in square only. In the same way D does not coincide with E.

**Step 4.** CE is not equal to DE. For suppose CE = DE. If C and D lie on the same side of E, then, AE being common, AC and AD are each obtained by subtracting the equals CE, DE from AE (or by adding them to AE), so AC = AD (CN3), and D coincides with C, contrary to D being another point. If C and D lie on opposite sides of E, say C between A and E and D between E and B, then AC = AE minus CE and DB = EB minus DE, and since AE = EB and CE = DE, AC = DB (CN3); hence, subtracting from the whole AB, AD = CB (CN3), contrary to Step 2. Therefore CE is not equal to DE; let CE be the greater (the argument is the same in the other case).

**Step 5.** Since the straight line AB is cut into equal segments at E and into unequal segments at C, the rectangle AC, CB together with the square on CE is equal to the square on AE (2.5). Likewise, AB being cut into unequal segments at D, the rectangle AD, DB together with the square on DE is equal to the square on AE (2.5). Therefore the rectangle AC, CB together with the square on CE is equal to the rectangle AD, DB together with the square on DE (CN1).

**Step 6.** Since CE is greater than DE, the square on CE is greater than the square on DE, for the square on DE, placed in the angle of the square on CE with sides along its sides, is a part of it (CN5). Let X be the area by which the square on CE exceeds the square on DE, so that the square on CE equals the square on DE together with X. Then the rectangle AC, CB together with the square on DE and X equals the rectangle AD, DB together with the square on DE; subtracting the square on DE from both (CN3), the rectangle AD, DB equals the rectangle AC, CB together with X. Thus the rectangle AD, DB exceeds the rectangle AC, CB by the area X.

**Step 7.** X is a rational area. Let K be the square on the assigned rational straight line. The rectangles AC, CB and AD, DB are rational, that is, each is commensurable with K (D10.1.4); hence they are commensurable with one another (10.12). Now the rectangle AD, DB is the sum of the rectangle AC, CB and X, and this whole is commensurable with the part, the rectangle AC, CB; therefore X is commensurable with the rectangle AC, CB (10.15). Consequently X is commensurable with K (10.12), that is, X is rational (D10.1.4).

**Step 8.** Twice X is also rational. Twice X has to X the ratio which the number 2 has to the number 1, so twice X is commensurable with X (10.6); hence twice X is commensurable with K (10.12), and is rational (D10.1.4).

**Step 9.** By 2.4, the square on AB equals the squares on AC, CB together with twice the rectangle AC, CB, and also equals the squares on AD, DB together with twice the rectangle AD, DB. From Step 6, adding equals to equals (CN2), twice the rectangle AD, DB equals twice the rectangle AC, CB together with twice X. Hence the squares on AC, CB together with twice the rectangle AC, CB equal the squares on AD, DB together with twice the rectangle AC, CB and twice X (CN1). Subtracting twice the rectangle AC, CB from both (CN3), the squares on AC, CB together equal the squares on AD, DB together with twice X. Thus the sum of the squares on AC, CB exceeds the sum of the squares on AD, DB by twice X, which is a rational area (Step 8).

**Step 10.** The sum of the squares on AC, CB is a medial area. Since AC, CB are commensurable in square, the squares on them are measured by the same area, so the square on AC is commensurable with the square on CB (D10.1.2, D10.1.1). Therefore the sum of the squares on AC, CB is commensurable with the square on AC (10.15). Now AC is medial, so the square on AC is the area called medial (10.21: a medial straight line is the side of a square equal to the rectangle contained by rational straight lines commensurable in square only). An area commensurable with a medial area is itself medial (10.23, Porism); therefore the sum of the squares on AC, CB is medial. In the same way, since AD, DB are medial and commensurable in square, the sum of the squares on AD, DB is medial.

**Step 11.** Therefore the medial area consisting of the squares on AC, CB exceeds the medial area consisting of the squares on AD, DB by the rational area twice X (Steps 9, 10). But a medial area does not exceed a medial area by a rational area (10.26). This is impossible; hence the supposition of Step 1 is false, and AB is not divided into two medial straight lines commensurable in square only containing a rational rectangle at any point other than C. Therefore a first bimedial straight line is divided at one point only. Q.E.D.

result.statement: A second bimedial straight line is divided at one point only.
result.proof:
**Statement:** A second bimedial straight line is divided at one point only.

**Step 1.** Let AB be a second bimedial straight line divided at C, so that AC, CB are medial straight lines commensurable in square only and containing a medial rectangle [10.38]. Suppose, if possible, that AB is also divided at a point D, different from C, so that AD, DB are likewise medial straight lines commensurable in square only and containing a medial rectangle, and that this division is not the same as the division at C; that is, AC is not equal to DB (and hence AD is not equal to CB either, the remainders of AB being unequal [CN3]).

**Step 2.** Since AC, CB are commensurable in square only, AC is incommensurable in length with CB [D10.1.2]; therefore AC is not equal to CB, for equal straight lines measure one another and so are commensurable [D10.1.1]. For the same reason AD is not equal to DB.

**Step 3.** Let a rational straight line EF be set out [D10.1.3], and to EF let there be applied, at right angles, the rectangle EK equal to the square on AB [1.45]; let EN be its other side, so that EK is the rectangle contained by EF, EN.

**Step 4.** Since AB is cut at C, the square on AB is equal to the squares on AC, CB together with twice the rectangle AC, CB [2.4]; so the squares on AC, CB are less than the square on AB, that is, than EK [CN5]. Let a rectangle EG equal to the squares on AC, CB be applied to EF [1.45], with its breadth EH placed along EN from E. Since EG is less than EK and both stand on EF, EH is less than EN (otherwise EK would be a part of EG or coincide with it, and EG would not be less [CN4, CN5]); so H lies between E and N. Let HK be the remaining rectangle, contained by EF, HN. Then HK, the excess of EK over EG, is equal to twice the rectangle AC, CB [2.4, CN3].

**Step 5.** In the same way, since AB is cut at D, the square on AB is equal to the squares on AD, DB together with twice the rectangle AD, DB [2.4]. Let EL, equal to the squares on AD, DB, be applied to EF with breadth EM along EN [1.45]; as before M lies between E and N, and the remaining rectangle MK, contained by EF, MN, is equal to twice the rectangle AD, DB [2.4, CN3].

**Step 6.** Since AC is medial, the square on AC is a medial area, being equal to a rectangle contained by rational straight lines commensurable in square only [10.21]. Since AC, CB are commensurable in square, the square on AC is commensurable with the square on CB [D10.1.2]; therefore the squares on AC, CB together are commensurable with the square on AC [10.15]. But an area commensurable with a medial area is medial [10.23, Porism]; therefore EG, which is equal to the squares on AC, CB, is a medial area, equal to the square on a medial straight line.

**Step 7.** EG is applied to the rational straight line EF and produces EH as breadth; therefore EH is rational and incommensurable in length with EF [10.22].

**Step 8.** The rectangle AC, CB is medial by hypothesis. Twice the rectangle AC, CB has to the rectangle AC, CB the ratio of 2 to 1, which is the ratio of a number to a number; therefore they are commensurable [10.6], and twice the rectangle AC, CB, that is HK, is medial [10.23, Porism]. HK is applied to EF and produces HN as breadth; therefore HN is rational and incommensurable in length with EF [10.22].

**Step 9.** The square on AC and the rectangle AC, CB are parallelograms under the same height AC standing on the bases AC, CB; therefore as AC is to CB, so is the square on AC to the rectangle AC, CB [6.1]. But AC is incommensurable in length with CB (Step 2); therefore the square on AC is incommensurable with the rectangle AC, CB [10.11].

**Step 10.** The squares on AC, CB are commensurable with the square on AC (Step 6), and the square on AC is incommensurable with the rectangle AC, CB; therefore the squares on AC, CB are incommensurable with the rectangle AC, CB [10.13]. Again, twice the rectangle AC, CB is commensurable with the rectangle AC, CB (Step 8); therefore the squares on AC, CB are incommensurable with twice the rectangle AC, CB [10.13]; that is, EG is incommensurable with HK.

**Step 11.** EG, HK are parallelograms under the same height EF standing on the bases EH, HN; therefore as EG is to HK, so is EH to HN [6.1]; and EG is incommensurable with HK; therefore EH is incommensurable in length with HN [10.11].

**Step 12.** EH is rational, that is, commensurable with EF either in length or in square only [D10.1.3]; and it is incommensurable in length with EF (Step 7); therefore it is commensurable in square with EF, so that the square on EH is commensurable with the square on EF [D10.1.2]. Likewise the square on HN is commensurable with the square on EF. Therefore the square on EH is commensurable with the square on HN [10.12], and EH, HN are commensurable in square [D10.1.2]. Being also incommensurable in length (Step 11), EH, HN are rational straight lines commensurable in square only; therefore EN, their sum, is a binomial straight line, divided into its terms at H [10.36].

**Step 13.** Further, EH is greater than HN. For AC, CB are unequal (Step 2); let AC be the greater, and from AC let a straight line equal to CB be cut off [1.3]. AC is then a straight line cut into a segment equal to CB and a remaining segment; therefore the square on AC together with the square on CB is equal to twice the rectangle contained by AC and CB together with the square on the remaining segment [2.7]. Hence the squares on AC, CB are greater than twice the rectangle AC, CB [CN5]; that is, EG is greater than HK. Both rectangles stand on EF; therefore EH is greater than HN (otherwise EG would be a part of HK or coincide with it, and would not be greater [CN4, CN5]). If CB is the greater, the same argument with CB in place of AC gives the same conclusion.

**Step 14.** AD, DB are also medial straight lines commensurable in square only containing a medial rectangle, and EL is equal to the squares on AD, DB while MK is equal to twice the rectangle AD, DB (Step 5). Therefore, repeating Steps 6 to 13 with AD, DB, EL, MK, EM, MN in place of AC, CB, EG, HK, EH, HN: EM and MN are rational straight lines commensurable in square only, so that EN is a binomial straight line divided into its terms also at M [10.36]; and EM is greater than MN.

**Step 15.** I say that H coincides with M. For if not, EH is not equal to EM. Nor is EH equal to MN: for then HN, the remainder of EN after EH, would be equal to EM, the remainder after MN [CN3]; and we should have EM equal to HN, HN less than EH (Step 13), EH equal to MN, and MN less than EM (Step 14), so that EM would be less than itself, which is absurd. Thus the terms EH, HN of the one division would be different from the terms EM, MN of the other, and the binomial straight line EN would be divided into its terms at two different points; but a binomial straight line is divided into its terms at one point only [10.42]. Therefore H coincides with M, EH is equal to EM, and the rectangles EG, EL contained by EF, EH and by EF, EM coincide and are equal [CN4]; that is, the squares on AC, CB are equal to the squares on AD, DB [CN1].

**Step 16.** Likewise HN coincides with MN, so that HK coincides with MK and they are equal [CN4]; therefore twice the rectangle AC, CB is equal to twice the rectangle AD, DB [CN1], and the rectangle AC, CB is equal to the rectangle AD, DB, being their halves.

**Step 17.** Let AB be bisected at O [1.10]. Since AC is not equal to CB (Step 2), C is not the point O; so AB is cut into equal segments at O and into unequal segments at C, and therefore the rectangle AC, CB together with the square on OC is equal to the square on AO [2.5]. Likewise, since AD is not equal to DB, D is not O, and the rectangle AD, DB together with the square on OD is equal to the square on AO [2.5].

**Step 18.** Therefore the rectangle AC, CB together with the square on OC is equal to the rectangle AD, DB together with the square on OD [CN1]; and the rectangles are equal (Step 16); therefore the square on OC is equal to the square on OD [CN3]. Hence OC is equal to OD; for if one of them were greater, the square on the other would be a part of the square on it, and the squares would be unequal [CN5].

**Step 19.** Now C, D are points of AB equidistant from O. They do not lie on the same side of O: for C, D being different points, one of OC, OD would then be a part of the other and less than it [CN5], whereas OC is equal to OD. Therefore they lie on opposite sides of O. If C lies towards B and D towards A, then AC is the sum of AO, OC and DB is the sum of DO, OB; and AO is equal to OB, OC to OD; therefore AC is equal to DB [CN2]. If instead C lies towards A and D towards B, then in the same way CB is equal to AD [CN2], and AC, DB, the remainders of AB, are equal [CN3]. In either case AC is equal to DB.

**Step 20.** But AC was supposed not equal to DB (Step 1): which is absurd. Therefore AB cannot be divided at a second point D into medial straight lines commensurable in square only containing a medial rectangle otherwise than as it is divided at C. Therefore a second bimedial straight line is divided at one point only. Q.E.D.

*Path note:* the proof reduces the question to the uniqueness of the division of the binomial EN [10.42]; the identity of the two divisions (EH = EM) is then carried back to AB through 2.4 and 2.5, which is more direct than first proving an inequality between the squares on AC, CB and on AD, DB.

result.statement: A major straight line is divided at one and the same point only.
result.proof:
**Step 1.** Let AB be a major straight line, divided at C into the two straight lines AC, CB from which it is compounded; that is (10.39), AC and CB are incommensurable in square, the sum of the squares on AC, CB is rational, and the rectangle AC·CB is medial. Throughout, an area is called rational when it is commensurable with the square on the assigned rational straight line (D10.1.4).

**Step 2.** Suppose, if possible, that AB is also divided at another point D, different from C, into straight lines AD, DB having the same properties: AD and DB incommensurable in square, the sum of the squares on AD, DB rational, and the rectangle AD·DB medial; and let the division at D be different from the division at C. Then AC is not equal to DB: for if AC = DB, then AD = CB (CN3), so that AD, DB would be the very same two straight lines CB, AC, and AB would be divided at D in the same way as at C, which is not a different division.

**Step 3.** Bisect AB at E (1.10). The point C is not E: for if C were E, then AC = CB, the squares on AC, CB would be equal and therefore measured by the same measure, that is, commensurable (D10.1.1), so that AC, CB would be commensurable in square (D10.1.2), contrary to Step 1. In the same way, D is not E. Hence AB is cut into equal segments at E and into unequal segments at C, and again into equal segments at E and into unequal segments at D.

**Step 4.** Therefore, by 2.5, the rectangle AC·CB together with the square on EC is equal to the square on AE, and the rectangle AD·DB together with the square on ED is equal to the square on AE. Hence (CN1) the rectangle AC·CB together with the square on EC is equal to the rectangle AD·DB together with the square on ED.

**Step 5.** EC is not equal to ED. For suppose EC = ED. Since C and D are different points at the same distance from E, they lie on opposite sides of E. If D lies between A and E and C between E and B, then AC = AE + EC and DB = EB + ED, and since AE = EB and EC = ED, AC = DB (CN2). If instead C lies between A and E and D between E and B, then CB = CE + EB = DE + EA = AD (CN2), whence AC = DB (CN3). Either case contradicts Step 2. Therefore EC and ED are unequal; and since the hypotheses concerning C and D are alike, let the lettering be so chosen that EC is greater than ED.

**Step 6.** Since EC > ED, the square on EC is greater than the square on ED. But by Step 4 the rectangle AC·CB together with the greater square (on EC) equals the rectangle AD·DB together with the less square (on ED). Therefore the rectangle AC·CB is less than the rectangle AD·DB, and consequently twice the rectangle AC·CB is less than twice the rectangle AD·DB. Let K be the excess of twice the rectangle AD·DB over twice the rectangle AC·CB, so that twice AD·DB = twice AC·CB + K.

**Step 7.** By 2.4, the square on AB is equal to the squares on AC, CB together with twice the rectangle AC·CB; and also the square on AB is equal to the squares on AD, DB together with twice the rectangle AD·DB. Hence (CN1) the squares on AC, CB together with twice AC·CB are equal to the squares on AD, DB together with twice AD·DB, that is, to the squares on AD, DB together with twice AC·CB and K. Taking away twice the rectangle AC·CB from each (CN3), the squares on AC, CB are equal to the squares on AD, DB together with K.

**Step 8.** K is rational. For the sum of the squares on AC, CB and the sum of the squares on AD, DB are both rational, that is, each is commensurable with the rational square set out (D10.1.4); therefore they are commensurable with one another (10.12). Now the whole, the sum of the squares on AC, CB, is made up of the sum of the squares on AD, DB and K (Step 7), and the whole is commensurable with the former part; therefore the parts, namely the sum of the squares on AD, DB and K, are commensurable with one another (10.15). Thus K is commensurable with the sum of the squares on AD, DB, which is commensurable with the rational square set out; therefore K is commensurable with the rational square set out (10.12), that is, K is rational (D10.1.4).

**Step 9.** Twice the rectangle AD·DB and twice the rectangle AC·CB are medial. For the rectangle AD·DB is medial (Step 2), and twice the rectangle AD·DB has to the rectangle AD·DB the ratio which the number 2 has to the unit, a ratio of a number to a number; therefore twice AD·DB is commensurable with AD·DB (10.6); and an area commensurable with a medial area is medial (10.23, Porism). Hence twice the rectangle AD·DB is medial; and in the same way twice the rectangle AC·CB is medial.

**Step 10.** By Step 6, twice the rectangle AD·DB is equal to twice the rectangle AC·CB together with K; that is, the medial area twice AD·DB exceeds the medial area twice AC·CB by the rational area K. But a medial area does not exceed a medial area by a rational area (10.26). This is impossible.

**Step 11.** Therefore AB cannot be divided at any point D other than C into two straight lines incommensurable in square whose squares have a rational sum and which contain a medial rectangle. Hence a major straight line is divided at one and the same point only. Q.E.D.

result.statement: The side of a rational plus a medial area is divided at one point only.
result.proof:
**Step 1.** Let AB be the side of a rational plus a medial area, divided at C, so that AC, CB are incommensurable in square, the sum of the squares on AC, CB is medial, and twice the rectangle AC, CB is rational [10.40]. Let R denote the square on the rational straight line set out, so that an area is rational precisely when it is commensurable with R [D10.1.4]. I say that AB is not divided at any other point into two straight lines having these properties.

**Step 2.** Suppose, if possible, that AB is also divided at another point D, so that AD, DB are incommensurable in square, the sum of the squares on AD, DB is medial, and twice the rectangle AD, DB is rational. "Another point" means a division different from that at C: D is not the same point as C, and moreover AC is not the same as DB. For if AC = DB, then, AB being the same whole in both divisions, the remainders CB and AD would be equal [CN3], and AB would be divided at D into the very same two straight lines as at C, merely interchanged; that is the same division, not a different one.

**Step 3.** Bisect AB at E [1.10]. Neither C nor D coincides with E. For if C were the point E, then AC = CB, so the squares on AC, CB would be equal and therefore measured by one and the same area (namely either of them); thus AC, CB would be commensurable in square [D10.1.2], contrary to hypothesis. In the same way D is not the point E.

**Step 4.** Further, C and D are not equidistant from E, that is, EC is not equal to ED. For suppose EC = ED. Since C is not the same point as D, the points C and D lie on opposite sides of E. If C lies between A and E and D between E and B, then AC is the remainder of AE after EC, and DB is the remainder of EB after ED; since AE = EB and EC = ED, it follows that AC = DB [CN3]. If instead C lies between E and B and D between A and E, then in the same way CB = AD, whence, subtracting these equals from the whole AB, AC = DB [CN3]. In either case AC = DB, which was excluded in Step 2. Therefore EC is not equal to ED.

**Step 5.** Since AB is cut into equal segments at E and into unequal segments at C, the rectangle AC, CB together with the square on EC is equal to the square on EB [2.5]. Similarly, since AB is cut into equal segments at E and into unequal segments at D, the rectangle AD, DB together with the square on ED is equal to the square on EB [2.5]. Therefore the rectangle AC, CB together with the square on EC is equal to the rectangle AD, DB together with the square on ED [CN1].

**Step 6.** Since EC is not equal to ED, the squares on EC, ED are unequal, the square on the less being equal to a part of the square on the greater [CN5]. Hence the rectangle AC, CB is not equal to the rectangle AD, DB; for otherwise, subtracting these equal rectangles from the equals of Step 5, the square on EC would be equal to the square on ED [CN3], which is not so. Consequently twice the rectangle AC, CB is not equal to twice the rectangle AD, DB. Since C and D satisfy exactly the same hypotheses, we may take twice the rectangle AC, CB to be the greater (otherwise interchange the roles of C and D). Let K be the area by which it exceeds, so that twice the rectangle AC, CB is equal to twice the rectangle AD, DB together with K.

**Step 7.** Since AB is cut at C, the square on AB is equal to the squares on AC, CB together with twice the rectangle AC, CB [2.4]; and since AB is cut at D, the square on AB is also equal to the squares on AD, DB together with twice the rectangle AD, DB [2.4]. Therefore the squares on AC, CB together with twice the rectangle AC, CB are equal to the squares on AD, DB together with twice the rectangle AD, DB [CN1].

**Step 8.** Replacing twice the rectangle AC, CB by its equal from Step 6, the squares on AC, CB together with twice the rectangle AD, DB and K are equal to the squares on AD, DB together with twice the rectangle AD, DB. Subtracting twice the rectangle AD, DB from both [CN3], the squares on AD, DB are equal to the squares on AC, CB together with K. That is, the sum of the squares on AD, DB exceeds the sum of the squares on AC, CB by the area K.

**Step 9.** The area K is rational. For twice the rectangle AC, CB and twice the rectangle AD, DB are both rational, so each is commensurable with R [D10.1.4]; being commensurable with the same area, they are commensurable with one another [10.12]. Now twice the rectangle AC, CB is the whole made up of the two parts, twice the rectangle AD, DB and K, and this whole is commensurable with one of the parts, twice the rectangle AD, DB; therefore the two parts, twice the rectangle AD, DB and K, are commensurable with one another [10.15]. Thus K is commensurable with twice the rectangle AD, DB, which is commensurable with R; hence K is commensurable with R [10.12], that is, K is rational [D10.1.4].

**Step 10.** But the sum of the squares on AD, DB is a medial area, and the sum of the squares on AC, CB is a medial area (Steps 1 and 2). Therefore, by Step 8, a medial area exceeds a medial area by the rational area K, which is impossible [10.26].

**Step 11.** Therefore the supposition of Step 2 is false: AB cannot be divided at any point other than C into two straight lines incommensurable in square which make the sum of the squares on them medial and twice the rectangle contained by them rational. Hence the side of a rational plus a medial area is divided at one point only. Q.E.D.

result.statement: The side of the sum of two medial areas is divided at one point only.
result.proof:
**Statement:** The side of the sum of two medial areas is divided at one point only.

**Step 1.** Let AB be the side of the sum of two medial areas, divided at C, so that AC, CB are incommensurable in square, the sum of the squares on AC, CB is medial, the rectangle AC·CB is medial, and the rectangle AC·CB is incommensurable with the sum of the squares on AC, CB [10.41]. Suppose, if possible, that AB is also divided at another point D fulfilling the same conditions — AD, DB incommensurable in square, the sum of the squares on AD, DB medial, the rectangle AD·DB medial and incommensurable with the sum of the squares on AD, DB — and that the division at D is not the same as that at C; that is, AD is not equal to CB (for if AD = CB, then DB = AC as well, and AB would be divided at D into the very same two segments as at C, which, exactly as in 10.42, is not a different division).

**Step 2.** Set out a rational straight line EF. To EF apply, in a right angle, the rectangle EG equal to the squares on AC, CB, its breadth being EH; and to the same EF (that is, to its equal HG), continuing along the same breadth, apply the rectangle HK equal to twice the rectangle AC·CB, its breadth being HN [1.44, 1.45]. Since the square on AB is equal to the squares on AC, CB together with twice the rectangle AC·CB [2.4], the whole rectangle EK, contained by EF and EN, is equal to the square on AB [CN2].

**Step 3.** Again, to EF apply the rectangle EL equal to the squares on AD, DB, its breadth being EM [1.44, 1.45]. Since the square on AB is equal to the squares on AD, DB together with twice the rectangle AD·DB [2.4], the squares on AD, DB are less than the square on AB [CN5]; so EL is less than EK, M falls between E and N, and the remainder LK, contained by ML (equal to EF) and MN, is equal to twice the rectangle AD·DB [CN3].

**Step 4.** EG is equal to the sum of the squares on AC, CB, which is medial; so EG is a medial area applied to the rational straight line EF, and therefore its breadth EH is rational and incommensurable in length with EF [10.22]. Again, twice the rectangle AC·CB is measured by the rectangle AC·CB, so the two are commensurable [D10.1.1]; and AC·CB is medial; therefore twice AC·CB is medial [10.23, Porism]. Thus HK is a medial area applied to the rational straight line EF, so that HN is rational and incommensurable in length with EF [10.22].

**Step 5.** The sum of the squares on AC, CB is incommensurable with the rectangle AC·CB, and AC·CB is commensurable with twice AC·CB (Step 4); therefore the sum of the squares on AC, CB is incommensurable with twice the rectangle AC·CB [10.13], that is, EG is incommensurable with HK. But EG, HK are parallelograms under the same height, so EG : HK = EH : HN [6.1]; therefore EH is incommensurable in length with HN [10.11].

**Step 6.** EH and HN are each rational, that is, each is commensurable with EF at least in square [D10.1.3], so that the square on EH and the square on HN are each commensurable with the square on EF [D10.1.2]; hence the square on EH is commensurable with the square on HN [10.12], that is, EH, HN are commensurable in square [D10.1.2]. Together with Step 5, EH, HN are rational straight lines commensurable in square only; therefore EN is a binomial straight line, divided into its terms EH, HN at the point H [10.36].

**Step 7.** In the same way for the division at M. EL is equal to the medial sum of the squares on AD, DB and is applied to the rational line EF, so EM is rational and incommensurable in length with EF [10.22]; twice the rectangle AD·DB is commensurable with the medial rectangle AD·DB [D10.1.1] and hence medial [10.23, Porism], so LK is a medial area applied to EF, and MN is rational and incommensurable in length with EF [10.22]; the sum of the squares on AD, DB is incommensurable with AD·DB and hence with twice AD·DB [10.13], so EL is incommensurable with LK, and, since EL : LK = EM : MN [6.1], EM is incommensurable in length with MN [10.11]; and the squares on EM, MN, each being commensurable with the square on EF [D10.1.3, D10.1.2], are commensurable with one another [10.12]. Therefore EM, MN are rational straight lines commensurable in square only, and EN is a binomial straight line divided into its terms EM, MN at the point M [10.36].

**Step 8.** Bisect AB at O [1.10]. The point C is not O; for if it were, AC would equal CB, the squares on AC, CB would be equal and so measured by one and the same area, and AC, CB would be commensurable in square [D10.1.2], contrary to hypothesis; likewise D is not O. So AB is cut into equal segments at O and into unequal segments at C; hence the squares on AC, CB are double of the squares on AO, OC [2.9], and the rectangle AC·CB together with the square on OC is equal to the square on AO [2.5]. Therefore the squares on AC, CB are equal to twice the rectangle AC·CB together with four times the square on OC [CN2], and so the sum of the squares on AC, CB is greater than twice the rectangle AC·CB [CN5]. In the same way the sum of the squares on AD, DB is greater than twice the rectangle AD·DB.

**Step 9.** The points H and M coincide. For suppose not; then EH is not equal to EM. Nor is EH equal to MN: for if EH = MN, then also HN = EM [CN3]; the rectangles EG, LK, being on the equal bases EH, MN and in the same parallels, would be equal, and likewise HK, EL [1.36]; that is, the squares on AC, CB would be equal to twice the rectangle AD·DB, and twice the rectangle AC·CB would be equal to the squares on AD, DB [CN1]; and then, by Step 8, the squares on AC, CB would be greater than twice AC·CB, which is equal to the squares on AD, DB, which are greater than twice AD·DB, which is equal to the squares on AC, CB — so that the squares on AC, CB would be greater than themselves, which is absurd. Hence, if H and M were distinct, the binomial EN would be divided into its terms in two different ways, at H into EH, HN and at M into EM, MN, where EM is equal neither to EH nor to HN; but a binomial straight line is divided into its terms at one point only [10.42]. Therefore H coincides with M.

**Step 10.** Since H and M coincide, EH = EM, and EG, EL are one and the same rectangle contained by EF, EH; therefore the sum of the squares on AC, CB is equal to the sum of the squares on AD, DB [CN1]. Each of these sums, together with twice the rectangle AC·CB and twice the rectangle AD·DB respectively, makes up the square on AB [2.4]; therefore twice AC·CB is equal to twice AD·DB [CN3], and hence the rectangle AC·CB is equal to the rectangle AD·DB, halves of equals being equal.

**Step 11.** By 2.5, the rectangle AC·CB together with the square on OC is equal to the square on AO, and the rectangle AD·DB together with the square on OD is equal to the same square on AO. Since the rectangles are equal (Step 10), the square on OC is equal to the square on OD [CN3]; hence OC = OD, for if one of them were greater, the square on it would contain the square on the other as a part and would be greater [CN5].

**Step 12.** Thus C and D lie on AB at the same distance OC from O. If they lie on the same side of O, they coincide, since otherwise one of OC, OD would be a part of the other and they could not be equal [CN5] — contrary to the supposition that D is another point. If they lie on opposite sides of O, say C between O and B and D between A and O, then AD = AO − OD = OB − OC = CB, and DB = OD + OB = OC + AO = AC [CN2, CN3, AO being equal to OB]; so AD = CB — contrary to the supposition that the division at D is different from that at C.

**Step 13.** In either case the supposition is impossible. Therefore AB cannot be divided in the required manner at any point other than C; that is, the side of the sum of two medial areas is divided at one point only. Q.E.D.

result.statement: To find the first binomial straight line.
result.proof:
**Step 1.** Let a rational straight line D be set out. Throughout, a straight line is called rational when it is commensurable with D, whether in length and in square or in square only (D10.1.3).

**Step 2.** By 10.29, let two rational straight lines A, B be found which are commensurable in square only, A being the greater, and such that the square on A is greater than the square on B by the square on a straight line C commensurable in length with A.

**Step 3.** Let EF be a straight line commensurable in length with D. Then EF is rational (D10.1.3).

**Step 4.** To the three given straight lines A, B, EF let a fourth proportional be found (6.12), and let it be FG, placed in a straight line with EF on the far side of F, so that as A is to B, so is EF to FG. Let EG be the whole straight line made up of EF and FG.

**Step 5.** Since A is greater than B, and as A is to B, so is EF to FG, therefore EF is greater than FG (5.14).

**Step 6.** Since A, B are commensurable in square only, A is incommensurable in length with B. And the four straight lines A, B, EF, FG are proportional; therefore EF is incommensurable in length with FG (10.11).

**Step 7.** Since as A is to B, so is EF to FG, the squares on them, being similar figures similarly described on four proportional straight lines, are also proportional: as the square on A is to the square on B, so is the square on EF to the square on FG (6.22). But A, B are commensurable in square, so the squares on A, B are measured by the same area (D10.1.2), that is, the square on A is commensurable with the square on B (D10.1.1). Therefore the square on EF is commensurable with the square on FG (10.11); that is, EF, FG are commensurable in square (D10.1.2).

**Step 8.** Since EF is commensurable in length with D, the square on EF has to the square on D the ratio which a square number has to a square number (10.9), and therefore the ratio which a number has to a number; hence the square on EF is commensurable with the square on D (10.6). But the square on FG is commensurable with the square on EF (Step 7). Therefore the square on FG is commensurable with the square on D (10.12), so that FG is commensurable in square with D (D10.1.2); therefore FG is rational (D10.1.3).

**Step 9.** Therefore EF, FG are rational straight lines (Steps 3, 8) commensurable in square (Step 7) but incommensurable in length (Step 6), that is, commensurable in square only. Therefore EG, the sum of EF and FG, is a binomial straight line (10.36), whose terms are EF and FG, and of which EF is the greater term (Step 5).

**Step 10.** Since the four straight lines A, B, EF, FG are proportional, and the square on the first, A, is greater than the square on the second, B, by the square on C, which is commensurable in length with A (Step 2), therefore the square on the third, EF, is also greater than the square on the fourth, FG, by the square on a straight line commensurable in length with EF (10.14).

**Step 11.** Thus EG is a binomial divided into its terms EF, FG at F; the square on the greater term EF is greater than the square on the lesser term FG by the square on a straight line commensurable in length with EF (Step 10); and the greater term EF is commensurable in length with the rational straight line D set out (Step 3). Therefore EG is a first binomial straight line (D10.2.1). Therefore the first binomial straight line EG has been found, which it was required to do.

Path note: the required pair of rational lines with the square-difference property is already supplied by 10.29; the most direct route is therefore to transfer that pair to a line commensurable in length with D by a fourth proportional, 10.14 carrying the square-difference property across the proportion and 10.11 carrying commensurability, rather than rebuilding the pair from a fresh choice of numbers.

result.statement: To find the second binomial straight line.
result.proof:
**Statement:** To find the second binomial straight line.

**Step 1.** Let D be the rational straight line set out (D10.1.3). Take two numbers AC, CB whose sum AB has to CB the ratio which a square number has to a square number, but has not to CA such a ratio: namely, let AB be the number 9, BC the number 4, and CA the number 5, so that AB is the sum of AC and CB. Since 9 is 3 multiplied by 3 and 4 is 2 multiplied by 2, AB and BC are square numbers (D7.18); therefore AB has to BC the ratio which a square number has to a square number. But AB has not to CA the ratio which a square number has to a square number: for if it had, then, AB being square, CA would also be square (8.24); but 5 is not a square number, since 2 by 2 makes 4 and 3 by 3 makes 9, and no number multiplied by itself makes 5.

**Step 2.** Let EF be a straight line commensurable in length with D. Then EF is rational (D10.1.3).

**Step 3.** Produce EF to G (P2) so that, as the number CA is to the number AB, so is the square on EF to the square on FG; this is possible by the Porism to 10.6 (a straight line X is found such that EF is to X as CA is to AB, and FG is taken as a mean proportional between EF and X, so that EF is to X as the square on EF is to the square on FG). Thus EG is one straight line divided at F.

**Step 4.** Since the square on EF has to the square on FG the ratio which the number CA has to the number AB, the square on EF is commensurable with the square on FG (10.6); that is, EF and FG are commensurable in square (D10.1.2).

**Step 5.** Since EF is commensurable in length with D, the square on EF has to the square on D the ratio which a square number has to a square number (10.9), and therefore the square on EF is commensurable with the square on D (10.6). But the square on FG is commensurable with the square on EF (Step 4). Therefore the square on FG is commensurable with the square on D (10.12), so that FG is commensurable in square with D and is therefore rational (D10.1.3).

**Step 6.** Since CA has not to AB the ratio which a square number has to a square number (Step 1), and the square on EF has to the square on FG the same ratio as CA has to AB (Step 3), neither has the square on EF to the square on FG the ratio which a square number has to a square number. Therefore EF is incommensurable in length with FG (10.9).

**Step 7.** Accordingly EF, FG are rational straight lines commensurable in square only (Steps 2, 4, 5, 6). Therefore EG, which is made up of them, is a binomial straight line, and EF, FG are its terms (10.36).

**Step 8.** Since, as CA is to AB, so is the square on EF to the square on FG, inversely, as AB is to CA, so is the square on FG to the square on EF (5.7 Porism). Now AB, being 9, is greater than CA, being 5. Take the same equimultiples of all four magnitudes, say the doubles: since AB is greater than CA, the double of AB exceeds the double of CA; hence, by the definition of magnitudes in the same ratio, the double of the square on FG exceeds the double of the square on EF (D5.5). Therefore the square on FG is greater than the square on EF, and consequently FG is greater than EF; so FG is the greater and EF the lesser of the two terms.

**Step 9.** On FG describe a semicircle FKG, and, since EF is less than FG, fit into it the straight line FK equal to EF (4.1); join KG (P1). The angle FKG, being in a semicircle, is right (3.31); therefore the square on FG is equal to the squares on FK, KG (1.47), that is, to the squares on EF, KG. Let H denote KG. Thus the square on FG is greater than the square on EF by the square on H.

**Step 10.** Since, as AB is to CA, so is the square on FG to the square on EF (Step 8), and AB exceeds CA by CB, while the square on FG exceeds the square on EF by the square on H (Step 9), convertendo, as AB is to BC, so is the square on FG to the square on H (5.19 Porism).

**Step 11.** But AB has to BC the ratio which a square number has to a square number (Step 1). Therefore the square on FG has to the square on H the ratio which a square number has to a square number, and hence FG is commensurable in length with H (10.9).

**Step 12.** Therefore EG is a binomial straight line divided into its terms EF, FG (Step 7); the square on the greater term FG is greater than the square on the lesser term EF by the square on H, a straight line commensurable in length with FG (Steps 9, 11); and the lesser term EF is commensurable in length with the rational straight line D set out (Step 2). Therefore EG is a second binomial straight line (D10.2.2). Thus the second binomial straight line EG has been found. Q.E.F.

**Path note.** The numbers were fixed explicitly (9, 4, 5) rather than by appeal to the unnumbered lemma after 10.28, and H was constructed by the semicircle method (the unnumbered lemma before 10.14) rather than cited, since lemmas carry no proposition numbers.

result.statement: To find the third binomial straight line.
result.proof:
**Step 1.** Set out two numbers AC, CB such that their sum AB has to BC the ratio which a square number has to a square number, but has not to AC the ratio which a square number has to a square number.

**Step 2.** Set out a further number D which is not square and has not to either of the numbers BA, AC the ratio which a square number has to a square number.

**Step 3.** Set out a rational straight line E (D10.1.3), and find a straight line FG such that, as the number D is to the number AB, so is the square on E to the square on FG (10.6, Porism).

**Step 4.** Since D : AB = (sq. on E) : (sq. on FG), the square on E has to the square on FG the ratio which a number has to a number; therefore the square on E is commensurable with the square on FG (10.6). Hence E and FG are commensurable in square (D10.1.2), and, E being rational, FG is rational (D10.1.3).

**Step 5.** Since D has not to AB the ratio which a square number has to a square number, neither has the square on E to the square on FG; therefore E is incommensurable in length with FG (10.9).

**Step 6.** Produce FG beyond G (P2), and cut off from the produced part a straight line GH such that, as the number BA is to the number AC, so is the square on FG to the square on GH (10.6 Porism, 1.3). Thus FG, GH lie in a straight line, and FH is their sum.

**Step 7.** Since BA : AC = (sq. on FG) : (sq. on GH), the square on FG is commensurable with the square on GH (10.6), so that FG, GH are commensurable in square (D10.1.2). But BA has not to AC the ratio which a square number has to a square number; therefore FG is incommensurable in length with GH (10.9).

**Step 8.** Since D : AB = (sq. on E) : (sq. on FG) and AB : AC = (sq. on FG) : (sq. on GH), ex aequali D : AC = (sq. on E) : (sq. on GH) (5.22). Therefore the square on E is commensurable with the square on GH (10.6), so that E, GH are commensurable in square (D10.1.2) and GH is rational (D10.1.3); and, since D has not to AC the ratio which a square number has to a square number, E is incommensurable in length with GH (10.9).

**Step 9.** Accordingly FG, GH are rational straight lines commensurable in square only (Steps 4, 7, 8); therefore the whole FH is a binomial straight line, divided into its terms FG, GH at the point G (10.36).

**Step 10.** Since AB is the sum of AC and CB, AB is greater than AC (CN5); and since BA : AC = (sq. on FG) : (sq. on GH), the square on FG is greater than the square on GH (5.14). Consequently FG is greater than GH (for otherwise the square on FG would not exceed the square on GH), and FG is the greater term of the binomial.

**Step 11.** Bisect FG at M (1.10), and with centre M and distance MF describe the semicircle FLG on FG (P3). Since GH is less than the diameter FG, fit into the semicircle a straight line FL equal to GH (4.1), and join LG (P1). The angle FLG, being in a semicircle, is right (3.31); therefore the square on FG is equal to the squares on FL, LG together (1.47). Denote LG by K; then the square on FG is equal to the squares on GH, K together, that is, the square on FG exceeds the square on GH by the square on K.

**Step 12.** Now AB : AC = (sq. on FG) : (sq. on GH), where AB is composed of AC, CB and the square on FG is composed of the squares on GH, K. Therefore, convertendo, AB : CB = (sq. on FG) : (sq. on K) (5.19, Porism).
